task_1_notices.title: Campus Study Lounge
task_1_notices.instruction: Read the notice and answer the question.
task_1_notices.passage:
CAMPUS STUDY LOUNGE
Due to acoustic refurbishment on Floor 2, individual silent booths will be temporarily closed until Thursday noon. Students requiring quiet study space may access Seminar Room 4B on Floor 3 without advance reservation. Group project discussions must relocate to the ground floor cafe.

questions.stem: 1. What does this notice tell students?

options.label: [A] They need to book Seminar Room 4B before using it.
[B] Alternative silent study space is accessible on Floor 3.
[C] Ground floor cafe facilities are closed for renovation.

questions.trap: [A] conflicts with 'without advance reservation'; [C] cafe is open for group work.

task_1_notices.title: Manuscript Reading Room
task_1_notices.instruction: Read the notice and answer the question.
task_1_notices.passage:
SPECIAL COLLECTIONS & ARCHIVES: MANUSCRIPT READING ROOM
Consultation of pre-1800 vellum documents requires clean cotton gloves, provided at the reception desk. Strictly no ink pens, highlighters, or liquids of any description may be brought past the security turnstile; only wooden graphite pencils are permitted for notation. Digital camera photography is permitted solely for registered researchers holding an approved reproduction permit.

questions.stem: 1. What are visitors to the Manuscript Reading Room instructed to do?

options.label: [A] Bring their own cotton gloves to inspect antique documents.
[B] Avoid bringing liquid writing instruments into the study space.
[C] Obtain prior written permission before using wooden graphite pencils.

questions.trap: [A] contradicts 'provided at reception'; [C] pencils are explicitly permitted.

task_1_notices.title: Heritage Letterpress Guild
task_1_notices.instruction: Read the notice and answer the question.
task_1_notices.passage:
HERITAGE LETTERPRESS GUILD: STUDIO WORKSHOP RULES
Due to the historic value of our movable lead and wooden display types, drawers must be re-shelved in their designated type cabinets immediately after typesetting. Solvents and linseed oil washes are restricted to the ventilation booth. Under no circumstances should type blocks be wiped with water, as moisture causes irreversible swelling of wooden sorts and corrosion of cast iron chases.

questions.stem: 1. What does the workshop notice tell guild members?

options.label: [A] Solvents are strictly banned from all areas of the studio.
[B] Cleaning type blocks with water is forbidden to prevent damage.
[C] Wooden display types must be cleaned before being returned to cabinets.

questions.trap: Cleaning type blocks with water is forbidden to prevent swelling of wood sorts.

task_1_notices.title: Corporate Facilities Advisory
task_1_notices.instruction: Read the notice and answer the question.
task_1_notices.passage:
CORPORATE FACILITIES ADVISORY
Annual acoustic testing of building alarm sounders will occur between 14:00 and 15:00 on Wednesday. Sirens will sound in ten-second intervals. Staff are NOT required to evacuate unless alarms ring continuously for over thirty seconds. Normal office work may proceed throughout the test window.

questions.stem: 1. What should employees do during Wednesday's alarm testing?

options.label: [A] Evacuate the premises immediately when any siren sounds.
[B] Continue working unless the alarm sounds without interruption.
[C] Assemble in designated ground floor meeting rooms at 14:00.

questions.trap: [A] conflicts with 'NOT required to evacuate unless alarms ring continuously'; [C] meeting not mentioned.

task_1_notices.title: Station Platform Notice
task_1_notices.instruction: Read the notice and answer the question.
task_1_notices.passage:
STATION PLATFORM ADVISORY
The passenger waiting lounge on Platform 2 is temporarily closed for floor maintenance. Heated shelters remain accessible on Platforms 1 and 3. Complimentary beverage vouchers are available from the customer assistance counter upon presentation of a valid rail travel card.

questions.stem: 1. What does this station notice announce to travellers?

options.label: [A] Waiting facilities remain accessible on alternative platforms.
[B] Free hot drinks are provided to all ticket holders on Platform 2.
[C] All platform shelters are closed until maintenance finishes.

questions.trap: [B] vouchers available at customer counter, not platform; [C] only Platform 2 lounge closed.

task_1_notices.title: Bicycle Shelter Regulations
task_1_notices.instruction: Read the notice and answer the question.
task_1_notices.passage:
COMMUTER BIKE STATION
All bicycles stored in the shelter must be registered with station security. Unregistered bicycles remaining in bays after 22:00 on Fridays will be impounded. Overnight parking is permitted only in designated bays on Level 2 with a valid electronic commuter permit.

questions.stem: 1. What does this notice tell readers?

options.label: [A] Bicycles left on weekends must have proper registration and permits.
[B] Any bicycle parked overnight will be permanently confiscated.
[C] Registration is optional for cyclists parking on Level 2.

questions.trap: [B] is too extreme; [C] registration is mandatory for all.

task_1_notices.title: Swimming Gala Closure Notice
task_1_notices.instruction: Read the notice and answer the question.
task_1_notices.passage:

task_1_notices.title: Allotment Water Restrictions

options.label: [A] Sprinkler irrigation is permitted during early morning hours.
[B] Plot holders must bring tap water from their own homes.
[C] Gardeners may only water crops using cans from rainwater barrels.

task_1_notices.title: Print Exhibition Extension

[B] Mei Lin's exhibition has been prolonged beyond its original dates.
[C] The gallery will be closed to visitors during weekday afternoons.

task_1_notices.title: Chemistry Lab Safety Memo
task_1_notices.instruction: Read the notice and answer the question.

options.label: [A] Solvents may be handled outside fume hoods if goggles are worn.
[B] Eating and drinking are strictly banned inside the synthesis laboratory.

task_1_notices.title: Metro Track Engineering Notice

task_1_notices.title: Medieval Vault Photography Rules

task_3_open_cloze.title: The Urban Forager
task_3_open_cloze.instruction: Read the text below and think of the word which best fits each gap. Use only ONE word in each gap.
task_3_open_cloze.passage:
For over a decade, botanical researcher Daniel Green has lived in central London, (3) _________ he leads guided foraging walks through city parks. Many people are astonished to discover how many edible plants thrive (4) _________ urban hedgerows and canal banks.

Daniel explains that prior to the Industrial Revolution, urban populations (5) _________ regularly gathered wild herbs and berries as a dietary supplement. Today, he aims to reconnect city dwellers with nature.

"Looking closely (6) _________ common weeds reveals a hidden culinary world," Daniel notes. He encourages participants to learn (7) _________ to distinguish nutritious greens from toxic lookalikes before picking anything.

questions.stem: Gap 3
questions.trap: 'which' requires preposition ('in which'). London is the spatial scene of leading walks.

questions.stem: Gap 4
questions.trap: Plants thrive 'in' hedgerows (medium / enclosure).

questions.stem: Gap 5
questions.trap: Past perfect auxiliary indicating customary historical practice prior to industrialization.

questions.stem: Gap 6
questions.trap: Dependent preposition: look closely 'at'.

questions.stem: Gap 7
questions.trap: Interrogative adverb of method: learn 'how' to distinguish.

task_3_open_cloze.title: The Book Town of Hay-on-Wye
task_3_open_cloze.instruction: Write ONE word only in each gap.
task_3_open_cloze.passage:
Nestled along the winding border between England and Wales lies Hay-on-Wye, a historic market town (3) _________ has earned global renown as the world's first open-air literary haven. In the early 1960s, an eccentric bibliophile named Richard Booth began buying dilapidated buildings and filling them (4) _________ salvaged antiquarian volumes from closing libraries.

Within two decades, dozens of specialty bookdealers followed suit, transforming sleepy residential lanes into a sprawling maze of open-air honesty bookshops. Visitors from across the world now wander through castle courtyards where shelves are left unattended overnight, (5) _________ relying on travelers to drop coins into wooden trust boxes.

"There is something magical (6) _________ discovering a forgotten 19th-century poetry volume in a ruined fortress," one regular traveler noted. Today, the town stands as living testament (7) _________ the enduring romance of the physical printed page.

questions.stem: Gap 3

task_5_extended_text.title: Filming on the Edge: Elena Vance
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the article about wildlife documentary filmmaker Elena Vance, and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
Wildlife filmmaker Elena Vance has spent twenty years capturing endangered fauna in the world's most inaccessible habitats. Raised in rural Scotland by naturalist parents, Elena developed an early reverence for the natural world. "My peers spent their teenage years glued to television screens," Elena recalls, "whereas I was tracking badger setts across frostbitten moorlands with my father's 35mm camera." After graduating with a zoology degree, she resisted the temptation of secure laboratory research, opting instead for freelance camerawork.

Her breakthrough arrived in 2012 while filming snow leopards in the high Pamir Mountains. Temperatures routinely plunged below minus thirty degrees Celsius, and weeks passed without a solitary sighting. "In wildlife cinematography, sheer technical brilliance counts for very little if you lack psychological endurance," Elena explains. "The camera operator who packs up after five shivering hours is the one who misses the two-second hunt that defines the entire series." Her perseverance was rewarded when she filmed an unprecedented sequence of a female leopard guiding two cubs across a glacial ridge.

Despite international acclaim, Elena remains critical of certain contemporary industry trends. In particular, she voices reservations about the growing reliance on computer-generated imagery (CGI) and digital sound enhancement in nature documentaries. "When producers artificially manipulate bird calls or amplify footsteps to heighten theatrical tension, they inadvertently sever the audience's genuine bond with reality," she asserts. "Spectators start expecting wildlife to behave like Hollywood actors, which breeds impatience toward authentic conservation efforts."

Today, Elena devotes substantial time to mentoring young filmmakers from biodiversity-rich developing nations. Through her mobile academy, she provides camera gear and storytelling workshops to aspiring directors across East Africa and Southeast Asia. "Indigenous observers possess intuitive ecological knowledge accumulated over generations," Elena concludes. "True conservation storytelling cannot simply be parachuted in by foreign production crews; it must be cultivated from within the communities who coexist with these ecosystems daily."

task_5_extended_text.title: The Granite Solitude of Dartmoor
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the memoir and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
For centuries, the desolate granite uplands of Dartmoor in southwest England have cast a somber spell over poets and wanderers. Clothed in purple heather, treacherous peat bogs, and eerie stone monuments dating back to the Bronze Age, this landscape resists human domestication. Last November, seeking respite from the frictionless routine of urban consulting, I packed a canvas rucksack and set out on a four-day solo trek across the north moor without GPS assistance, relying strictly on an Ordnance Survey contour map and an antique brass compass.

By mid-afternoon on my second day, an impenetrable blanket of Atlantic sea-fog rolled silently across the tors. Within minutes, visible landmarks vanished. In such disorienting isolation, every sensory stimulus contracts to the immediate radius of your boots: the squelch of saturated moss beneath wet leather, the sharp whistling of cold gale-force winds through granite crevices, and the brooding silence of the hills. You are no longer a detached observer consuming scenery, but a humble organism navigating raw geological antiquity.

Navigating Dartmoor's infamous mire beds demands rigorous vigilance. What appears to be an inviting patch of bright emerald turf is frequently a deceitful "quaking bog"—a liquid slurry of subterranean silt and decomposed peat. Learning to read subtle botanical indicators became my lifeline: avoidance of fluorescent mosses, following the sturdy hoof-paths carved by wild semi-feral ponies, and probing suspicious ground with a seasoned hazel walking stick.

As dusk settled on the final evening, I reached the ancient oak woodland of Wistman’s Wood. Here, dwarf pedunculate oaks have grown for millennia, their gnarled, moss-encrusted branches contorted like petrified sea serpents between colossal boulders. Standing amidst this primeval cathedral, I was struck by how contemporary society has banished darkness and silence from daily life. We congratulate ourselves on instantaneous digital connectivity, yet we have severed our ancestral relationship with the unhurried rhythms of the earth. Dartmoor does not flatter human self-importance; it humbles our hurried ambitions and reminds us of the profound restorative dignity found in quiet endurance.

task_5_extended_text.title: Echoes from the Ice Margin
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the Arctic field memoir and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
Svalbard in late September is a landscape rendered in charcoal, slate, and bone. As our three-person glaciological survey team pitched our geodesic tent upon the gravelly terminal moraine of the Nordenskiöld Glacier, the temperature was already descending toward minus fifteen. We had journeyed to this remote high-Arctic fjord not to measure surface melting with orbital radars, but to document something far more elusive: the internal acoustic and structural memory of ancient ice.

Most people imagine glaciers as inert, frozen monuments. In reality, an active glacier is an animate, restless organism in perpetual motion. Throughout the polar night, the ice fabric groans under immense tectonic pressures. As we hammered seismic listening stakes into the glacier’s snout, the ground vibrated with concussive snaps and low-frequency resonant thrums. These acoustic pulses represent the release of strain energy accumulated over hundreds of years of compaction. To sit alone in total Arctic stillness and listen to a glacier exhale is an experience of terrifying majesty.

On our fourth morning, a sudden katabatic storm ripped down the valley off the inland ice cap, howling at sixty knots and reducing visibility to arm's length in stinging spindrift. For forty-eight hours, our fragile nylon shelter was our entire universe. Confined to our sleeping bags, cooking over a sputtering kerosene stove, we were forced into a state of acute mental endurance. In such extreme isolation, one's perception of time expands; the frantic urgency that governs contemporary metropolitan life is shown to be a trivial illusion against the monumental timescales of the polar wilderness.

When the storm finally spent itself, we emerged into a world bathed in eerie golden twilight. The newly cleared air revealed fresh calving scarps along the glacier’s marine terminus, towering cliffs of turquoise ice that had sheared off into the fjord during the blizzard. Extracting ice core samples from these exposed strata was like reading an illuminated manuscript of prehistoric atmospheres. As I held a translucent core cylinder toward the low Arctic sun, watching tiny ancient atmospheres effervesce in my palm, I felt an overpowering blend of scientific awe and acute grief for a frozen heritage disappearing before our eyes.

task_5_extended_text.title: Algorithmic Translation and Sociolinguistic Nuance
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the academic essay on artificial intelligence and sociolinguistics, and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
In recent years, neural machine translation (NMT) architectures have achieved unprecedented fluency in standard written registers. Leveraging transformer-based large language models trained on billions of bilingual sentence pairs, contemporary translation engines navigate syntactic inversions and technical vocabularies with remarkable statistical precision. However, computational sociolinguists caution that this apparent technical triumph masks a profound vulnerability: the inability of algorithmic systems to interpret dialectal variation, localized idioms, and pragmatic implicature.

Language is rarely a neutral vehicle for transmuting propositional logic; rather, it functions as an intricate index of social identity, regional heritage, and class allegiance. When machine translation engines process vernacular dialects—such as African American Vernacular English (AAVE), Scots, or Singlish—they routinely stumble over non-standard grammatical markers. For example, the habitual 'be' in AAVE conveys an aspectual nuance of recurring action that standard English accomplishes through auxiliary adverbials. Algorithms trained almost exclusively on sanitized parliamentary proceedings and corporate press releases frequently mistranslate habitual 'be' as a momentary present state, inadvertently flattening crucial temporal distinctions.

This linguistic blind spot creates what sociolinguists term 'epistemic flattening'. By defaulting to hegemonic national standards whenever ambiguity arises, algorithmic translation platforms subtly discourage linguistic diversity. In global commercial and legal environments where machine translation is deployed as a cost-effective triage tool, communications framed in regional vernaculars risk being flagged as erroneous or unprofessional. Consequently, speakers of marginalized dialects face systematic communicative friction, pressured to abandon their heritage varieties in favor of algorithms-friendly standard dialects.

Professional human translators observe that post-editing machine-generated output for non-standard prose is frequently more labor-intensive than translating from scratch. While statistical engines excel at syntactic parsing, they lack the embodied cultural knowledge required to decipher sarcasm, double entendres, and community-specific honorifics. Until computational models incorporate ethnographic context and sociolinguistic sensitivity, translation must remain fundamentally rooted in human interpretation.

[C] Its sluggish operational speed when analyzing long texts.

task_5_extended_text.title: Urban Soundscape Ecology & Architectural Psychoacoustics
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the architectural analysis on urban sound design, and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
For more than a century, municipal approaches to urban sound have been defined by an obsession with acoustic elimination. Noise abatement ordinances, heavy roadside sound barriers, and triple-glazed windows all operate under a singular premise: that the acoustic signature of the city is an inherent pollutant that must be extinguished. However, a growing cohort of architectural psychoacousticians argues that this decibel-reduction paradigm is fundamentally flawed. Complete silence in dense metropolitan spaces is not only physically unachievable, but psychologically disorienting for human occupants.

Soundscape ecology posits that the quality and composition of sonic stimuli exert far greater influence on human neurophysiology than absolute volume alone. While intermittent, unpredictable mechanical impulses—such as sirens, pneumatic drills, and accelerating exhaust systems—trigger immediate cortisol surges and sympathetic nervous arousal, continuous natural sounds produce the opposite effect. Biophilic acoustic interventions, such as cascade fountains, rustling ornamental grasses, and engineered wind corridors, introduce stochastic 'pink noise' that effectively masks harsh mechanical transients without raising overall sound pressure.

Recent residential trials in Amsterdam and Singapore have substantiated this thesis through biometric monitoring. In experimental housing blocks retrofitted with acoustic soundscape landscaping—including porous basalt facades and acoustic vegetated balconies—residents reported a thirty percent reduction in subjective stress and exhibited significantly lower nighttime heart rate variability spikes. Remarkably, ambient acoustic monitors confirmed that exterior decibel levels remained virtually identical to control blocks; the crucial difference lay in the acoustic spectral texture.

Nevertheless, urban developers routinely resist integrating psychoacoustic landscaping into early project phases. Acoustic engineering is frequently treated as an afterthought, relegated to remedial insulation once structural framing is already locked in. Pioneering practitioners argue that cities must transition from reactionary noise mitigation to proactive acoustic curation, designing public squares and transit plazas where sound is sculpted as intentionally as light and shadow.

[D] They exempt commercial delivery vehicles from quiet-hour regulations.

[D] By completely isolating buildings from outdoor atmospheric currents.

task_5_extended_text.title: Filming on the Edge: Elena Vance [Variant 6]
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the article about wildlife documentary filmmaker Elena Vance, and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
Wildlife filmmaker Elena Vance has spent twenty years capturing endangered fauna in the world's most inaccessible habitats. Raised in rural Scotland by naturalist parents, Elena developed an early reverence for the natural world. "My peers spent their teenage years glued to television screens," Elena recalls, "whereas I was tracking badger setts across frostbitten moorlands with my father's 35mm camera." After graduating with a zoology degree, she resisted the temptation of secure laboratory research, opting instead for freelance camerawork.

Her breakthrough arrived in 2012 while filming snow leopards in the high Pamir Mountains. Temperatures routinely plunged below minus thirty degrees Celsius, and weeks passed without a solitary sighting. "In wildlife cinematography, sheer technical brilliance counts for very little if you lack psychological endurance," Elena explains. "The camera operator who packs up after five shivering hours is the one who misses the two-second hunt that defines the entire series." Her perseverance was rewarded when she filmed an unprecedented sequence of a female leopard guiding two cubs across a glacial ridge.

Despite international acclaim, Elena remains critical of certain contemporary industry trends. In particular, she voices reservations about the growing reliance on computer-generated imagery (CGI) and digital sound enhancement in nature documentaries. "When producers artificially manipulate bird calls or amplify footsteps to heighten theatrical tension, they inadvertently sever the audience's genuine bond with reality," she asserts. "Spectators start expecting wildlife to behave like Hollywood actors, which breeds impatience toward authentic conservation efforts."

Today, Elena devotes substantial time to mentoring young filmmakers from biodiversity-rich developing nations. Through her mobile academy, she provides camera gear and storytelling workshops to aspiring directors across East Africa and Southeast Asia. "Indigenous observers possess intuitive ecological knowledge accumulated over generations," Elena concludes. "True conservation storytelling cannot simply be parachuted in by foreign production crews; it must be cultivated from within the communities who coexist with these ecosystems daily."

task_5_extended_text.title: Algorithmic Translation and Sociolinguistic Nuance [Variant 9]
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the academic essay on artificial intelligence and sociolinguistics, and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
In recent years, neural machine translation (NMT) architectures have achieved unprecedented fluency in standard written registers. Leveraging transformer-based large language models trained on billions of bilingual sentence pairs, contemporary translation engines navigate syntactic inversions and technical vocabularies with remarkable statistical precision. However, computational sociolinguists caution that this apparent technical triumph masks a profound vulnerability: the inability of algorithmic systems to interpret dialectal variation, localized idioms, and pragmatic implicature.

Language is rarely a neutral vehicle for transmuting propositional logic; rather, it functions as an intricate index of social identity, regional heritage, and class allegiance. When machine translation engines process vernacular dialects—such as African American Vernacular English (AAVE), Scots, or Singlish—they routinely stumble over non-standard grammatical markers. For example, the habitual 'be' in AAVE conveys an aspectual nuance of recurring action that standard English accomplishes through auxiliary adverbials. Algorithms trained almost exclusively on sanitized parliamentary proceedings and corporate press releases frequently mistranslate habitual 'be' as a momentary present state, inadvertently flattening crucial temporal distinctions.

This linguistic blind spot creates what sociolinguists term 'epistemic flattening'. By defaulting to hegemonic national standards whenever ambiguity arises, algorithmic translation platforms subtly discourage linguistic diversity. In global commercial and legal environments where machine translation is deployed as a cost-effective triage tool, communications framed in regional vernaculars risk being flagged as erroneous or unprofessional. Consequently, speakers of marginalized dialects face systematic communicative friction, pressured to abandon their heritage varieties in favor of algorithms-friendly standard dialects.

Professional human translators observe that post-editing machine-generated output for non-standard prose is frequently more labor-intensive than translating from scratch. While statistical engines excel at syntactic parsing, they lack the embodied cultural knowledge required to decipher sarcasm, double entendres, and community-specific honorifics. Until computational models incorporate ethnographic context and sociolinguistic sensitivity, translation must remain fundamentally rooted in human interpretation.

task_5_extended_text.title: Urban Soundscape Ecology & Architectural Psychoacoustics [Variant 10]
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the architectural analysis on urban sound design, and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
For more than a century, municipal approaches to urban sound have been defined by an obsession with acoustic elimination. Noise abatement ordinances, heavy roadside sound barriers, and triple-glazed windows all operate under a singular premise: that the acoustic signature of the city is an inherent pollutant that must be extinguished. However, a growing cohort of architectural psychoacousticians argues that this decibel-reduction paradigm is fundamentally flawed. Complete silence in dense metropolitan spaces is not only physically unachievable, but psychologically disorienting for human occupants.

Soundscape ecology posits that the quality and composition of sonic stimuli exert far greater influence on human neurophysiology than absolute volume alone. While intermittent, unpredictable mechanical impulses—such as sirens, pneumatic drills, and accelerating exhaust systems—trigger immediate cortisol surges and sympathetic nervous arousal, continuous natural sounds produce the opposite effect. Biophilic acoustic interventions, such as cascade fountains, rustling ornamental grasses, and engineered wind corridors, introduce stochastic 'pink noise' that effectively masks harsh mechanical transients without raising overall sound pressure.

Recent residential trials in Amsterdam and Singapore have substantiated this thesis through biometric monitoring. In experimental housing blocks retrofitted with acoustic soundscape landscaping—including porous basalt facades and acoustic vegetated balconies—residents reported a thirty percent reduction in subjective stress and exhibited significantly lower nighttime heart rate variability spikes. Remarkably, ambient acoustic monitors confirmed that exterior decibel levels remained virtually identical to control blocks; the crucial difference lay in the acoustic spectral texture.

Nevertheless, urban developers routinely resist integrating psychoacoustic landscaping into early project phases. Acoustic engineering is frequently treated as an afterthought, relegated to remedial insulation once structural framing is already locked in. Pioneering practitioners argue that cities must transition from reactionary noise mitigation to proactive acoustic curation, designing public squares and transit plazas where sound is sculpted as intentionally as light and shadow.

task_5_extended_text.title: Filming on the Edge: Elena Vance [Variant 11]
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the article about wildlife documentary filmmaker Elena Vance, and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
Wildlife filmmaker Elena Vance has spent twenty years capturing endangered fauna in the world's most inaccessible habitats. Raised in rural Scotland by naturalist parents, Elena developed an early reverence for the natural world. "My peers spent their teenage years glued to television screens," Elena recalls, "whereas I was tracking badger setts across frostbitten moorlands with my father's 35mm camera." After graduating with a zoology degree, she resisted the temptation of secure laboratory research, opting instead for freelance camerawork.

Her breakthrough arrived in 2012 while filming snow leopards in the high Pamir Mountains. Temperatures routinely plunged below minus thirty degrees Celsius, and weeks passed without a solitary sighting. "In wildlife cinematography, sheer technical brilliance counts for very little if you lack psychological endurance," Elena explains. "The camera operator who packs up after five shivering hours is the one who misses the two-second hunt that defines the entire series." Her perseverance was rewarded when she filmed an unprecedented sequence of a female leopard guiding two cubs across a glacial ridge.

Despite international acclaim, Elena remains critical of certain contemporary industry trends. In particular, she voices reservations about the growing reliance on computer-generated imagery (CGI) and digital sound enhancement in nature documentaries. "When producers artificially manipulate bird calls or amplify footsteps to heighten theatrical tension, they inadvertently sever the audience's genuine bond with reality," she asserts. "Spectators start expecting wildlife to behave like Hollywood actors, which breeds impatience toward authentic conservation efforts."

Today, Elena devotes substantial time to mentoring young filmmakers from biodiversity-rich developing nations. Through her mobile academy, she provides camera gear and storytelling workshops to aspiring directors across East Africa and Southeast Asia. "Indigenous observers possess intuitive ecological knowledge accumulated over generations," Elena concludes. "True conservation storytelling cannot simply be parachuted in by foreign production crews; it must be cultivated from within the communities who coexist with these ecosystems daily."

task_5_extended_text.title: The Granite Solitude of Dartmoor [Variant 12]
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the memoir and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
For centuries, the desolate granite uplands of Dartmoor in southwest England have cast a somber spell over poets and wanderers. Clothed in purple heather, treacherous peat bogs, and eerie stone monuments dating back to the Bronze Age, this landscape resists human domestication. Last November, seeking respite from the frictionless routine of urban consulting, I packed a canvas rucksack and set out on a four-day solo trek across the north moor without GPS assistance, relying strictly on an Ordnance Survey contour map and an antique brass compass.

By mid-afternoon on my second day, an impenetrable blanket of Atlantic sea-fog rolled silently across the tors. Within minutes, visible landmarks vanished. In such disorienting isolation, every sensory stimulus contracts to the immediate radius of your boots: the squelch of saturated moss beneath wet leather, the sharp whistling of cold gale-force winds through granite crevices, and the brooding silence of the hills. You are no longer a detached observer consuming scenery, but a humble organism navigating raw geological antiquity.

Navigating Dartmoor's infamous mire beds demands rigorous vigilance. What appears to be an inviting patch of bright emerald turf is frequently a deceitful "quaking bog"—a liquid slurry of subterranean silt and decomposed peat. Learning to read subtle botanical indicators became my lifeline: avoidance of fluorescent mosses, following the sturdy hoof-paths carved by wild semi-feral ponies, and probing suspicious ground with a seasoned hazel walking stick.

As dusk settled on the final evening, I reached the ancient oak woodland of Wistman’s Wood. Here, dwarf pedunculate oaks have grown for millennia, their gnarled, moss-encrusted branches contorted like petrified sea serpents between colossal boulders. Standing amidst this primeval cathedral, I was struck by how contemporary society has banished darkness and silence from daily life. We congratulate ourselves on instantaneous digital connectivity, yet we have severed our ancestral relationship with the unhurried rhythms of the earth. Dartmoor does not flatter human self-importance; it humbles our hurried ambitions and reminds us of the profound restorative dignity found in quiet endurance.

task_5_extended_text.title: Echoes from the Ice Margin [Variant 13]
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the Arctic field memoir and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
Svalbard in late September is a landscape rendered in charcoal, slate, and bone. As our three-person glaciological survey team pitched our geodesic tent upon the gravelly terminal moraine of the Nordenskiöld Glacier, the temperature was already descending toward minus fifteen. We had journeyed to this remote high-Arctic fjord not to measure surface melting with orbital radars, but to document something far more elusive: the internal acoustic and structural memory of ancient ice.

Most people imagine glaciers as inert, frozen monuments. In reality, an active glacier is an animate, restless organism in perpetual motion. Throughout the polar night, the ice fabric groans under immense tectonic pressures. As we hammered seismic listening stakes into the glacier’s snout, the ground vibrated with concussive snaps and low-frequency resonant thrums. These acoustic pulses represent the release of strain energy accumulated over hundreds of years of compaction. To sit alone in total Arctic stillness and listen to a glacier exhale is an experience of terrifying majesty.

On our fourth morning, a sudden katabatic storm ripped down the valley off the inland ice cap, howling at sixty knots and reducing visibility to arm's length in stinging spindrift. For forty-eight hours, our fragile nylon shelter was our entire universe. Confined to our sleeping bags, cooking over a sputtering kerosene stove, we were forced into a state of acute mental endurance. In such extreme isolation, one's perception of time expands; the frantic urgency that governs contemporary metropolitan life is shown to be a trivial illusion against the monumental timescales of the polar wilderness.

When the storm finally spent itself, we emerged into a world bathed in eerie golden twilight. The newly cleared air revealed fresh calving scarps along the glacier’s marine terminus, towering cliffs of turquoise ice that had sheared off into the fjord during the blizzard. Extracting ice core samples from these exposed strata was like reading an illuminated manuscript of prehistoric atmospheres. As I held a translucent core cylinder toward the low Arctic sun, watching tiny ancient atmospheres effervesce in my palm, I felt an overpowering blend of scientific awe and acute grief for a frozen heritage disappearing before our eyes.

task_5_extended_text.title: Filming on the Edge: Elena Vance [Variant 16]
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the article about wildlife documentary filmmaker Elena Vance, and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
Wildlife filmmaker Elena Vance has spent twenty years capturing endangered fauna in the world's most inaccessible habitats. Raised in rural Scotland by naturalist parents, Elena developed an early reverence for the natural world. "My peers spent their teenage years glued to television screens," Elena recalls, "whereas I was tracking badger setts across frostbitten moorlands with my father's 35mm camera." After graduating with a zoology degree, she resisted the temptation of secure laboratory research, opting instead for freelance camerawork.

Her breakthrough arrived in 2012 while filming snow leopards in the high Pamir Mountains. Temperatures routinely plunged below minus thirty degrees Celsius, and weeks passed without a solitary sighting. "In wildlife cinematography, sheer technical brilliance counts for very little if you lack psychological endurance," Elena explains. "The camera operator who packs up after five shivering hours is the one who misses the two-second hunt that defines the entire series." Her perseverance was rewarded when she filmed an unprecedented sequence of a female leopard guiding two cubs across a glacial ridge.

Despite international acclaim, Elena remains critical of certain contemporary industry trends. In particular, she voices reservations about the growing reliance on computer-generated imagery (CGI) and digital sound enhancement in nature documentaries. "When producers artificially manipulate bird calls or amplify footsteps to heighten theatrical tension, they inadvertently sever the audience's genuine bond with reality," she asserts. "Spectators start expecting wildlife to behave like Hollywood actors, which breeds impatience toward authentic conservation efforts."

Today, Elena devotes substantial time to mentoring young filmmakers from biodiversity-rich developing nations. Through her mobile academy, she provides camera gear and storytelling workshops to aspiring directors across East Africa and Southeast Asia. "Indigenous observers possess intuitive ecological knowledge accumulated over generations," Elena concludes. "True conservation storytelling cannot simply be parachuted in by foreign production crews; it must be cultivated from within the communities who coexist with these ecosystems daily."

task_5_extended_text.title: The Granite Solitude of Dartmoor [Variant 17]
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the memoir and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
For centuries, the desolate granite uplands of Dartmoor in southwest England have cast a somber spell over poets and wanderers. Clothed in purple heather, treacherous peat bogs, and eerie stone monuments dating back to the Bronze Age, this landscape resists human domestication. Last November, seeking respite from the frictionless routine of urban consulting, I packed a canvas rucksack and set out on a four-day solo trek across the north moor without GPS assistance, relying strictly on an Ordnance Survey contour map and an antique brass compass.

By mid-afternoon on my second day, an impenetrable blanket of Atlantic sea-fog rolled silently across the tors. Within minutes, visible landmarks vanished. In such disorienting isolation, every sensory stimulus contracts to the immediate radius of your boots: the squelch of saturated moss beneath wet leather, the sharp whistling of cold gale-force winds through granite crevices, and the brooding silence of the hills. You are no longer a detached observer consuming scenery, but a humble organism navigating raw geological antiquity.

Navigating Dartmoor's infamous mire beds demands rigorous vigilance. What appears to be an inviting patch of bright emerald turf is frequently a deceitful "quaking bog"—a liquid slurry of subterranean silt and decomposed peat. Learning to read subtle botanical indicators became my lifeline: avoidance of fluorescent mosses, following the sturdy hoof-paths carved by wild semi-feral ponies, and probing suspicious ground with a seasoned hazel walking stick.

As dusk settled on the final evening, I reached the ancient oak woodland of Wistman’s Wood. Here, dwarf pedunculate oaks have grown for millennia, their gnarled, moss-encrusted branches contorted like petrified sea serpents between colossal boulders. Standing amidst this primeval cathedral, I was struck by how contemporary society has banished darkness and silence from daily life. We congratulate ourselves on instantaneous digital connectivity, yet we have severed our ancestral relationship with the unhurried rhythms of the earth. Dartmoor does not flatter human self-importance; it humbles our hurried ambitions and reminds us of the profound restorative dignity found in quiet endurance.

task_5_extended_text.title: Echoes from the Ice Margin [Variant 18]
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the Arctic field memoir and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
Svalbard in late September is a landscape rendered in charcoal, slate, and bone. As our three-person glaciological survey team pitched our geodesic tent upon the gravelly terminal moraine of the Nordenskiöld Glacier, the temperature was already descending toward minus fifteen. We had journeyed to this remote high-Arctic fjord not to measure surface melting with orbital radars, but to document something far more elusive: the internal acoustic and structural memory of ancient ice.

Most people imagine glaciers as inert, frozen monuments. In reality, an active glacier is an animate, restless organism in perpetual motion. Throughout the polar night, the ice fabric groans under immense tectonic pressures. As we hammered seismic listening stakes into the glacier’s snout, the ground vibrated with concussive snaps and low-frequency resonant thrums. These acoustic pulses represent the release of strain energy accumulated over hundreds of years of compaction. To sit alone in total Arctic stillness and listen to a glacier exhale is an experience of terrifying majesty.

On our fourth morning, a sudden katabatic storm ripped down the valley off the inland ice cap, howling at sixty knots and reducing visibility to arm's length in stinging spindrift. For forty-eight hours, our fragile nylon shelter was our entire universe. Confined to our sleeping bags, cooking over a sputtering kerosene stove, we were forced into a state of acute mental endurance. In such extreme isolation, one's perception of time expands; the frantic urgency that governs contemporary metropolitan life is shown to be a trivial illusion against the monumental timescales of the polar wilderness.

When the storm finally spent itself, we emerged into a world bathed in eerie golden twilight. The newly cleared air revealed fresh calving scarps along the glacier’s marine terminus, towering cliffs of turquoise ice that had sheared off into the fjord during the blizzard. Extracting ice core samples from these exposed strata was like reading an illuminated manuscript of prehistoric atmospheres. As I held a translucent core cylinder toward the low Arctic sun, watching tiny ancient atmospheres effervesce in my palm, I felt an overpowering blend of scientific awe and acute grief for a frozen heritage disappearing before our eyes.

task_5_extended_text.title: Algorithmic Translation and Sociolinguistic Nuance [Variant 19]
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the academic essay on artificial intelligence and sociolinguistics, and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
In recent years, neural machine translation (NMT) architectures have achieved unprecedented fluency in standard written registers. Leveraging transformer-based large language models trained on billions of bilingual sentence pairs, contemporary translation engines navigate syntactic inversions and technical vocabularies with remarkable statistical precision. However, computational sociolinguists caution that this apparent technical triumph masks a profound vulnerability: the inability of algorithmic systems to interpret dialectal variation, localized idioms, and pragmatic implicature.

Language is rarely a neutral vehicle for transmuting propositional logic; rather, it functions as an intricate index of social identity, regional heritage, and class allegiance. When machine translation engines process vernacular dialects—such as African American Vernacular English (AAVE), Scots, or Singlish—they routinely stumble over non-standard grammatical markers. For example, the habitual 'be' in AAVE conveys an aspectual nuance of recurring action that standard English accomplishes through auxiliary adverbials. Algorithms trained almost exclusively on sanitized parliamentary proceedings and corporate press releases frequently mistranslate habitual 'be' as a momentary present state, inadvertently flattening crucial temporal distinctions.

This linguistic blind spot creates what sociolinguists term 'epistemic flattening'. By defaulting to hegemonic national standards whenever ambiguity arises, algorithmic translation platforms subtly discourage linguistic diversity. In global commercial and legal environments where machine translation is deployed as a cost-effective triage tool, communications framed in regional vernaculars risk being flagged as erroneous or unprofessional. Consequently, speakers of marginalized dialects face systematic communicative friction, pressured to abandon their heritage varieties in favor of algorithms-friendly standard dialects.

Professional human translators observe that post-editing machine-generated output for non-standard prose is frequently more labor-intensive than translating from scratch. While statistical engines excel at syntactic parsing, they lack the embodied cultural knowledge required to decipher sarcasm, double entendres, and community-specific honorifics. Until computational models incorporate ethnographic context and sociolinguistic sensitivity, translation must remain fundamentally rooted in human interpretation.

task_5_extended_text.title: Urban Soundscape Ecology & Architectural Psychoacoustics [Variant 20]
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the architectural analysis on urban sound design, and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
For more than a century, municipal approaches to urban sound have been defined by an obsession with acoustic elimination. Noise abatement ordinances, heavy roadside sound barriers, and triple-glazed windows all operate under a singular premise: that the acoustic signature of the city is an inherent pollutant that must be extinguished. However, a growing cohort of architectural psychoacousticians argues that this decibel-reduction paradigm is fundamentally flawed. Complete silence in dense metropolitan spaces is not only physically unachievable, but psychologically disorienting for human occupants.

Soundscape ecology posits that the quality and composition of sonic stimuli exert far greater influence on human neurophysiology than absolute volume alone. While intermittent, unpredictable mechanical impulses—such as sirens, pneumatic drills, and accelerating exhaust systems—trigger immediate cortisol surges and sympathetic nervous arousal, continuous natural sounds produce the opposite effect. Biophilic acoustic interventions, such as cascade fountains, rustling ornamental grasses, and engineered wind corridors, introduce stochastic 'pink noise' that effectively masks harsh mechanical transients without raising overall sound pressure.

Recent residential trials in Amsterdam and Singapore have substantiated this thesis through biometric monitoring. In experimental housing blocks retrofitted with acoustic soundscape landscaping—including porous basalt facades and acoustic vegetated balconies—residents reported a thirty percent reduction in subjective stress and exhibited significantly lower nighttime heart rate variability spikes. Remarkably, ambient acoustic monitors confirmed that exterior decibel levels remained virtually identical to control blocks; the crucial difference lay in the acoustic spectral texture.

Nevertheless, urban developers routinely resist integrating psychoacoustic landscaping into early project phases. Acoustic engineering is frequently treated as an afterthought, relegated to remedial insulation once structural framing is already locked in. Pioneering practitioners argue that cities must transition from reactionary noise mitigation to proactive acoustic curation, designing public squares and transit plazas where sound is sculpted as intentionally as light and shadow.

[D] By completely isolating buildings from outdoor atmospheric currents.

We had journeyed to this remote high-Arctic fjord not to measure surface melting with orbital radars, but to document something far more elusive: the internal acoustic and structural memory of ancient ice.

Most people imagine glaciers as inert, frozen monuments. In reality, an active glacier is an animate, restless organism in perpetual motion. Throughout the polar night, the ice fabric groans under immense tectonic pressures. As we hammered seismic listening stakes into the glacier’s snout, the ground vibrated with concussive snaps and low-frequency resonant thrums. These acoustic pulses represent the release of strain energy accumulated over hundreds of years of compaction. To sit alone in total Arctic stillness and listen to a glacier exhale is an experience of terrifying majesty.

On our fourth morning, a sudden katabatic storm ripped down the valley off the inland ice cap, howling at sixty knots and reducing visibility to arm's length in stinging spindrift. For forty-eight hours, our fragile nylon shelter was our entire universe. Confined to our sleeping bags, cooking over a sputtering kerosene stove, we were forced into a state of acute mental endurance. In such extreme isolation, one's perception of time expands; the frantic urgency that governs contemporary metropolitan life is shown to be a trivial illusion against the monumental timescales of the polar wilderness.

When the storm finally spent itself, we emerged into a world bathed in eerie golden twilight. The newly cleared air revealed fresh calving scarps along the glacier’s marine terminus, towering cliffs of turquoise ice that had sheared off into the fjord during the blizzard. Extracting ice core samples from these exposed strata was like reading an illuminated manuscript of prehistoric atmospheres. As I held a translucent core cylinder toward the low Arctic sun, watching tiny ancient atmospheres effervesce in my palm, I felt an overpowering blend of scientific awe and acute grief for a frozen heritage disappearing before our eyes.

[B] To investigate internal acoustic stresses and structural behaviors within the ice.
[C] To evaluate whether high-Arctic moraines can support permanent scientific bases.

task_5_extended_text.title: Algorithmic Translation and Sociolinguistic Nuance [Variant 24]
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the academic essay on artificial intelligence and sociolinguistics, and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
In recent years, neural machine translation (NMT) architectures have achieved unprecedented fluency in standard written registers. Leveraging transformer-based large language models trained on billions of bilingual sentence pairs, contemporary translation engines navigate syntactic inversions and technical vocabularies with remarkable statistical precision. However, computational sociolinguists caution that this apparent technical triumph masks a profound vulnerability: the inability of algorithmic systems to interpret dialectal variation, localized idioms, and pragmatic implicature.

Language is rarely a neutral vehicle for transmuting propositional logic; rather, it functions as an intricate index of social identity, regional heritage, and class allegiance. When machine translation engines process vernacular dialects—such as African American Vernacular English (AAVE), Scots, or Singlish—they routinely stumble over non-standard grammatical markers. For example, the habitual 'be' in AAVE conveys an aspectual nuance of recurring action that standard English accomplishes through auxiliary adverbials. Algorithms trained almost exclusively on sanitized parliamentary proceedings and corporate press releases frequently mistranslate habitual 'be' as a momentary present state, inadvertently flattening crucial temporal distinctions.

This linguistic blind spot creates what sociolinguists term 'epistemic flattening'. By defaulting to hegemonic national standards whenever ambiguity arises, algorithmic translation platforms subtly discourage linguistic diversity. In global commercial and legal environments where machine translation is deployed as a cost-effective triage tool, communications framed in regional vernaculars risk being flagged as erroneous or unprofessional. Consequently, speakers of marginalized dialects face systematic communicative friction, pressured to abandon their heritage varieties in favor of algorithms-friendly standard dialects.

Professional human translators observe that post-editing machine-generated output for non-standard prose is frequently more labor-intensive than translating from scratch. While statistical engines excel at syntactic parsing, they lack the embodied cultural knowledge required to decipher sarcasm, double entendres, and community-specific honorifics. Until computational models incorporate ethnographic context and sociolinguistic sensitivity, translation must remain fundamentally rooted in human interpretation.

options.label: [A] Its reliance on outdated grammatical parsing models.
[B] Its inability to process sociolinguistic and contextual subtleties.
[C] Its sluggish operational speed when analyzing long texts.
[D] Its frequent generation of severe syntactic errors in formal registers.

task_5_extended_text.title: Urban Soundscape Ecology & Architectural Psychoacoustics [Variant 25]
task_5_extended_text.instruction: Read the architectural analysis on urban sound design, and answer questions 13–17.
task_5_extended_text.passage:
For more than a century, municipal approaches to urban sound have been defined by an obsession with acoustic elimination. Noise abatement ordinances, heavy roadside sound barriers, and triple-glazed windows all operate under a singular premise: that the acoustic signature of the city is an inherent pollutant that must be extinguished. However, a growing cohort of architectural psychoacousticians argues that this decibel-reduction paradigm is fundamentally flawed. Complete silence in dense metropolitan spaces is not only physically unachievable, but psychologically disorienting for human occupants.

Soundscape ecology posits that the quality and composition of sonic stimuli exert far greater influence on human neurophysiology than absolute volume alone. While intermittent, unpredictable mechanical impulses—such as sirens, pneumatic drills, and accelerating exhaust systems—trigger immediate cortisol surges and sympathetic nervous arousal, continuous natural sounds produce the opposite effect. Biophilic acoustic interventions, such as cascade fountains, rustling ornamental grasses, and engineered wind corridors, introduce stochastic 'pink noise' that effectively masks harsh mechanical transients without raising overall sound pressure.

Recent residential trials in Amsterdam and Singapore have substantiated this thesis through biometric monitoring. In experimental housing blocks retrofitted with acoustic soundscape landscaping—including porous basalt facades and acoustic vegetated balconies—residents reported a thirty percent reduction in subjective stress and exhibited significantly lower nighttime heart rate variability spikes. Remarkably, ambient acoustic monitors confirmed that exterior decibel levels remained virtually identical to control blocks; the crucial difference lay in the acoustic spectral texture.

Nevertheless, urban developers routinely resist integrating psychoacoustic landscaping into early project phases. Acoustic engineering is frequently treated as an afterthought, relegated to remedial insulation once structural framing is already locked in. Pioneering practitioners argue that cities must transition from reactionary noise mitigation to proactive acoustic curation, designing public squares and transit plazas where sound is sculpted as intentionally as light and shadow.

options.label: [A] They spend municipal budgets on unproven digital audio technologies.

[C] They fail to inspect older residential apartment buildings.
[D] They exempt commercial delivery vehicles from quiet-hour regulations.

[D] By completely isolating buildings from outdoor atmospheric currents.

[B] Proactive acoustic curation alongside visual architecture

task_6_short_article.title: The Psychology of Clutter
task_6_short_article.instruction: Read the short article on environmental psychology, and answer questions 18–19.
task_6_short_article.passage:
Modern domestic environments are increasingly inundated with consumer possessions. While material abundance is widely equated with prosperity, cognitive psychologists have revealed that excessive domestic clutter exerts a measurable toll on emotional well-being. Neuroimaging studies demonstrate that cluttered physical environments overload the visual cortex, severely impeding the brain’s capacity to process information and regulate stress hormones.

Intriguingly, the psychological impact of clutter is markedly asymmetrical across genders and personality types. Individuals who identify strongly with home management report elevated cortisol levels when surrounded by disorganization, perceiving unaddressed items not merely as physical objects, but as a persistent backlog of unfinished duties. Conversely, those who reframe domestic possessions as sources of historical continuity or creative stimuli remain relatively impervious to clutter-induced anxiety.

questions.stem: 18. According to the first paragraph, how does clutter affect mental performance?

options.label: [A] It causes individuals to spend excessive time searching for lost possessions.
[B] It strains sensory processing systems, diminishing cognitive clarity.
[C] It prompts households to purchase larger, unaffordable living spaces.
[D] It disrupts sleep patterns through heightened chemical sensitivity.

questions.trap: Paragraph 1: 'cluttered physical environments overload the visual cortex, severely impeding...'.

questions.stem: 19. What explains why some individuals remain unaffected by domestic clutter?

options.label: [A] They maintain organized storage solutions behind closed doors.
[B] They possess different subjective perceptions of their possessions' value.
[C] They delegate domestic responsibilities to other household members.
[D] They spend significantly less time inside their residential homes.

questions.trap: Paragraph 2: 'reframe domestic possessions as sources of historical continuity or creative stimuli'.

task_6_short_article.title: The Architecture of Scent and Memory
task_6_short_article.instruction: Read the short article and answer questions 18–19.
task_6_short_article.passage: Few cognitive experiences are as sudden and emotionally vivid as the involuntary recollection triggered by an unexpected scent. Termed the "Proustian phenomenon"—after Marcel Proust's celebrated description of a tea-soaked madeleine unleashing childhood memories—this sensory superpower has distinct evolutionary roots. Unlike visual or auditory signals, which pass through the thalamus for cognitive filtering before reaching higher cortical regions, olfactory nerves connect directly to the amygdala and hippocampus, the neurobiological centers governing emotion and associative memory. Because this direct neurological pathway bypasses analytical deliberation, scents evoke memories with unparalleled emotional immediacy and sensory fidelity.

questions.stem: 18. According to the first paragraph, why do smells trigger memories more instantly than sounds or sights?

options.label: [A] Human nostrils possess significantly more receptor cells than the eyes or ears.
[B] Olfactory signals travel directly to emotional brain centers without prior analytical filtering.
[C] Scents are processed during deep stages of sleep when memory consolidation occurs.
[D] Auditory memories deteriorate at a much faster rate over the human lifespan.

questions.trap: Direct pathway to amygdala/hippocampus without thalamic filtering.

questions.stem: 19. What characterizes the memories awakened by the "Proustian phenomenon"?

options.label: [A] They tend to focus exclusively on traumatic childhood warnings.
[B] They possess an intense emotional atmosphere and remarkably clear sensory detail.
[C] They require repeated exposure to the scent before they can be unlocked.
[D] They are easily altered or distorted by modern adult preconceptions.

questions.trap: Evokes memories with unparalleled emotional immediacy and sensory fidelity.

task_6_short_article.title: The Cognitive Value of Solitude
task_6_short_article.instruction: Read the short article and answer questions 18–19.
task_6_short_article.passage: In a hyper-connected culture where being alone is pathologized as loneliness, developmental psychologists are rediscovering the value of deliberate solitude. While involuntary isolation can provoke distress, intentional solitude functions as a crucial cognitive crucible for personal growth, self-regulation, and creative breakthrough. Cognitive neuroscientists note that constant social interaction activates the "executive control network." When an individual steps away into quiet seclusion, the brain smoothly transitions to the "default mode network." This neural state facilitates autobiographical memory integration, divergent problem-solving, and existential self-reflection. Far from an empty void, solitude is the mental space where intellectual autonomy takes root.

questions.stem: 18. According to the first paragraph, how does intentional solitude differ from loneliness?

options.label: [A] It can only be practiced in remote outdoor natural environments.
[B] It is an active, chosen condition that fosters creative renewal and cognitive resilience.
[C] It requires complete sensory deprivation to achieve therapeutic effects.
[D] It is exclusively beneficial for individuals with introverted personalities.

questions.trap: Active chosen condition that fosters personal growth and creative breakthrough.

questions.stem: 19. What neurological shift happens when a person enters solitary quietude?

options.label: [A] The brain shuts down memory recall to preserve metabolic energy.
[B] The executive control network increases in speed to solve logical dilemmas.
[C] Brain activity shifts toward the default mode network, enabling deeper reflection.
[D] Sensory nerve receptors become hyper-sensitive to external acoustic stimuli.

questions.trap: Brain transitions to default mode network, facilitating autobiographical reflection.

task_6_short_article.title: Cognitive Ergonomics & Asynchronous Work
task_6_short_article.instruction: Read the short article on workplace psychology, and answer questions 18–19.
task_6_short_article.passage:
The transition to decentralized, remote employment has elevated asynchronous communication platforms—such as team messaging applications and collaborative project boards—to organizational staples. Proponents celebrate the freedom from rigid real-time meetings, arguing that asynchronous workflows empower personnel to operate during their individual peak cognitive hours. However, occupational psychologists have identified an insidious counter-phenomenon: the chronic fragmentation of attention.

When team members receive an unpredictable trickle of notifications throughout the working day, the brain remains in a perpetual state of hyper-vigilance. Rather than entering periods of sustained, uninterrupted deep work, knowledge workers switch cognitive tasks an average of once every four minutes. This rapid alternation depletes executive functioning, elevating perceived exhaustion even when objective workload volumes remain moderate. Workplace researchers recommend that enterprises establish clear 'notification-free batching windows' to restore mental stamina.

questions.stem: 18. According to the first paragraph, what is the main advantage claimed for asynchronous communication?

options.label: [A] It eliminates the financial cost of leasing corporate headquarters.
[B] It allows individuals to schedule work around their optimal mental performance.
[C] It prevents project deadlines from being extended by managers.
[D] It guarantees that international workers receive immediate responses.

questions.trap: [B] matches 'empower personnel to operate during their individual peak cognitive hours'.

questions.stem: 19. What problem does the author associate with unpredictable daytime notifications?

options.label: [A] They cause employees to make severe computational errors in financial spreadsheets.
[B] They keep the nervous system continuously on alert and shatter uninterrupted focus.
[C] They cause home Wi-Fi networks to suffer severe bandwidth slowdowns.
[D] They encourage employees to work unpaid overtime during night hours.

questions.trap: [B] matches 'brain remains in a perpetual state of hyper-vigilance... switch cognitive tasks an average of once every four minutes'.

task_6_short_article.title: Extremophile Enzymes in Abyssal Hydrothermal Vents
task_6_short_article.instruction: Read the short article on marine biotechnology, and answer questions 18–19.
task_6_short_article.passage:
Deep-sea hydrothermal vents, spewing mineral-laden fluids at temperatures exceeding 350 degrees Celsius under hydrostatic pressures of several hundred atmospheres, were long assumed to be sterile oceanic wastelands. In reality, these abyssal fissures host flourishing ecosystems driven by chemosynthetic extremophiles. Microorganisms known as hyperthermophiles not only survive in these hostile environments, but thrive by utilizing specialized enzymes termed 'extremozymes' whose rigid protein architectures resist thermal denaturation.

Biotechnologists and industrial biochemists are intensely interested in these molecular structures. Standard commercial enzymes utilized in pharmaceutical synthesis, textile bleaching, and biofuel production rapidly degrade when exposed to elevated temperatures or corrosive acidities, necessitating costly cooling systems and chemical stabilizers. Extremozymes derived from vent bacteria operate with peak catalytic efficiency precisely under these punishing conditions, offering a sustainable, energy-efficient path toward green industrial manufacturing.

questions.stem: 18. What molecular feature enables vent microorganisms to endure superheated water?

options.label: [A] Highly flexible cellular membranes that absorb excess ambient moisture.
[B] Unusually rigid enzyme structures that prevent proteins from unravelling.
[C] The ability to enter a dormant spore state until temperatures decline.
[D] External mineral shells that completely block boiling fluids.

questions.trap: [B] matches 'rigid protein architectures resist thermal denaturation'.

questions.stem: 19. Why are commercial manufacturers seeking to utilize extremozymes?

options.label: [A] They eliminate the need for expensive cooling and chemical stabilization in industrial processes.
[B] They can be harvested cheaply in vast quantities from surface ocean water.
[C] They are already certified as non-toxic by international food agencies.
[D] They replace human machine operators in automated pharmaceutical factories.

questions.trap: [A] matches 'necessitating costly cooling systems and chemical stabilizers... offering a sustainable path'.

task_7_gapped_sentences.title: Living Lanterns of the Deep
task_7_gapped_sentences.instruction: Read the text about bioluminescence. Choose the correct sentence from A–H to fit each gap (20–24).
task_7_gapped_sentences.passage:
In the pitch-black waters of the deep ocean, sunlight disappears entirely beyond two hundred meters. Yet this abyssal zone is far from completely dark; it sparkles with an astonishing array of living light. Bioluminescence—the biochemical production of light by living organisms—is not a rare curiosity, but the dominant mode of communication in the pelagic realm. (20) [ _________ ].

The chemical reaction powering this illumination typically involves two components: a light-emitting pigment called luciferin and an enzyme known as luciferase. When catalyzed in the presence of oxygen, this reaction releases almost ninety-eight percent of its energy as visible cold light, generating virtually no wasted heat. (21) [ _________ ]. In the open ocean, blue-green wavelengths travel farthest through seawater, which explains why the overwhelming majority of marine light displays conform to this color spectrum.

Marine creatures deploy bioluminescence for a wide spectrum of survival strategies. Many predatory anglerfish dangle glowing fleshy lures directly above their needle-sharp jaws to entice unsuspecting prey. (22) [ _________ ]. By emitting faint light from their bellies that precisely matches the intensity and wavelength of downwelling sunlight, midwater squid render their silhouettes invisible to predators lurking beneath them.

Other species utilize sudden, blinding flashes as an emergency defensive smokescreen. Deep-sea comb jellies and brittle stars discharge clouds of glowing mucus to disorient attackers while they make their escape. (23) [ _________ ]. This alarm summons even larger apex predators to attack the initial assailant, effectively saving the glowing prey in the chaos.

Today, biomedical researchers are adapting these natural light-generating systems for human healthcare. By inserting jellyfish bioluminescent genes into human cancer cells, oncologists can track tumor growth and evaluate drug effectiveness in real time under specialized microscopes. (24) [ _________ ]. What began as an evolutionary adaptation in deep-sea obscurity has transformed into an indispensable beacon illuminating modern medicine.

[A] In some cases, this luminous display functions as a "burglar alarm" that attracts secondary predators.
[B] This thermal efficiency outstrips even the most advanced human-engineered LED technologies.
[C] In contrast, terrestrial fireflies utilize green-yellow flashes primarily for nocturnal courtship displays.
[D] Marine mammals, such as sperm whales, have never been observed producing bioluminescent chemicals.
[E] Marine scientists estimate that more than three-quarters of all midwater animals possess light-generating organs.
[F] Commercial fisheries frequently deploy synthetic chemical glow-sticks to attract schooling tuna.
[G] Similar genetic techniques are now being piloted to monitor wastewater contamination and bacterial pathogens.
[H] Equally widespread is the defensive tactic of counter-illumination camouflage.

task_7_gapped_sentences.title: The Phantom Islands of Early Sea Charts
task_7_gapped_sentences.instruction: Choose the correct sentence (A–H) for each gap (20–24).
task_7_gapped_sentences.passage:
For hundreds of years, maritime navigators set sail across open oceans guided by maps depicting islands that did not exist. These elusive geographic ghosts occupied prominent positions on European charts from the fourteenth through the nineteenth centuries. (20) [ _________ ].

One famous example was Hy-Brasil, an enigmatic island said to lie west of Ireland. Celtic folklore held that it was perpetually cloaked in dense mists, revealing its shores once every seven years. (21) [ _________ ]. Admiralty charts marked its coordinates well into the Victorian era, as captains mistook low-hanging cloud banks for land.

Another enduring phantom was the island of Saint Brendan, named after a sixth-century Irish monk who sailed into the western ocean. Medieval cartographers placed Brendan's paradise across various Atlantic locations. (22) [ _________ ]. When Columbus set sail in 1492, his crew kept a vigilant watch for Brendan’s island as a provisioning post.

One famous example was Hy-Brasil, an enigmatic island said to lie west of Ireland. Celtic folklore held that it was perpetually cloaked in dense mists, revealing its shores once every seven years. (21) [ _________ ]. Admiralty charts marked its coordinates well into the Victorian era, as captains mistook low-hanging cloud banks for land.

Another enduring phantom was the island of Saint Brendan, named after a sixth-century Irish monk who sailed into the western ocean. Medieval cartographers placed Brendan's paradise across various Atlantic locations. (22) [ _________ ]. When Columbus set sail in 1492, his crew kept a vigilant watch for Brendan’s island as a provisioning post.

The persistence of these landmasses was not purely imagination; navigation was plagued by dead reckoning errors. (23) [ _________ ]. Furthermore, mapmakers faced intense commercial pressure to produce comprehensive charts; omitting an island claimed by a celebrated captain could ruin an atlas maker's reputation.

The ultimate demise of phantom islands arrived with the marine chronometer and systematic hydrographic surveying. (24) [ _________ ]. Yet, even today, these vanished archipelagos retain an enduring allure, reminding us of an era when the edges of maps were still inscribed with mystery.
task_7_gapped_sentences.optionsReference:
Options:
[A] Over time, rigorous naval expeditions methodically combed the Atlantic, erasing these mythical coordinates from official charts.
[B] Modern satellite imagery has uncovered hidden volcanic peaks beneath these precise ocean coordinates.
[C] Far from being deliberate hoaxes, they were born of mirages, navigational miscalculations, and sailors' desperate hopes.
[D] Deep-sea divers frequently discover sunken stone masonry beneath the shallow sandbanks of the Celtic Sea.
[E] Despite repeated voyages failing to locate its anchorages, cartographers refused to strike it from their copperplate engravings.
[F] Consequently, an isolated iceberg, a floating mat of pumice, or a distant bank of fog was easily logged as newly discovered territory.
[G] European monarchs issued royal charters claiming sovereignty over these mythical territories.
[H] Even when Spanish expeditions proved the Caribbean was land, Brendan's haven merely migrated further west on newer maps.

task_7_gapped_sentences.title: The Silent Labor of the Scriptoria [Variant 13]
task_7_gapped_sentences.instruction: Choose the correct sentence (A–H) for each gap (20–24).
task_7_gapped_sentences.passage:
Long before Gutenberg introduced movable type, every book had to be written letter by letter by hand. In the drafty stone cloisters of medieval monasteries, devoted scribes spent decades hunched over tilted oak desks in designated workshops known as scriptoria. (20) [ _________ ].

Working conditions in monastic scriptoria were Spartan. Rules strictly prohibited heating fires or tallow candles anywhere near desks, for fear that a spark could incinerate irreplaceable volumes. (23) [ _________ ]. Yet despite this punishing labor, master illuminators decorated margins with breathtaking gold leaf and lapis lazuli miniatures.

Today, preserved medieval manuscripts represent some of humanity's most breathtaking physical treasures. (24) [ _________ ]. They stand as living monuments to the astonishing patience of craftsmen who dedicated lifetimes to safeguarding the fragile flame of knowledge.

task_7_gapped_sentences.title: The Chemistry of Illuminated Manuscript Preservation [Variant 14]
task_7_gapped_sentences.instruction: Read the text about historical manuscript conservation. Choose the correct sentence from A–G to fit each gap (20–24). There are two extra sentences.
task_7_gapped_sentences.passage:
Medieval illuminated manuscripts represent some of humanity's most visually stunning and fragile cultural artifacts. Crafted from animal vellum and decorated with ground mineral pigments and gold leaf, these books have survived for centuries in monastic vaults. (20) [ _________ ]. As conservation science matures, specialists are turning to non-destructive chemical analysis to decelerate this deterioration.

One of the primary agents of destruction is iron gall ink, which served as the standard writing medium across Europe from the Middle Ages through the nineteenth century. Created by combining iron sulfate with oak gall extracts, the ink produces a rich, durable dark line. (21) [ _________ ]. Over centuries, excess sulfuric acid eats entirely through the vellum substrate, causing text lines to crumble into brittle lacework.

To combat this corrosive pathway, conservators previously bathed entire folios in chemical neutralizing washes. (22) [ _________ ]. Early aqueous immersions frequently caused organic binder adhesives to dissolve, leading to catastrophic flaking of delicate illuminated gilding.

Modern preservation protocols therefore avoid invasive chemical baths whenever possible. Instead, technicians deploy non-invasive portable X-ray fluorescence (XRF) spectroscopy to map elemental distributions across the ink without physical contact. (23) [ _________ ]. Armed with this quantitative diagnostic map, conservators can pinpoint precisely which areas require micro-targeted antioxidant consolidation.

Environmental climate control remains the final, and most critical, line of defense. By maintaining storage vaults at a strict forty-five percent relative humidity and fifteen degrees Celsius, institutions prevent both vellum cockling and fungal germination. (24) [ _________ ]. Through this convergence of chemistry and microclimate management, these ancient voices will endure for future generations.

[F] Many collectors prefer rebinding ancient manuscripts with modern embossed leather covers.
