task_7_gapped_sentences.title: Precision Agroforestry and Soil Mycorrhizal Networks [Variant 15]
task_7_gapped_sentences.instruction: Read the text about sustainable agriculture and forestry. Choose the correct sentence from A–G to fit each gap (20–24). There are two extra sentences.
task_7_gapped_sentences.passage:
For decades, conventional industrial agriculture has relied on intensive monoculture cropping sustained by artificial nitrogen fertilizers and chemical fungicides. While this model initially delivered high crop yields, it has severely depleted topsoil biodiversity worldwide. (20) [ _________ ]. By integrating deep-rooted perennial trees directly into arable crop fields, farmers are restoring subterranean ecological synergy.

The foundational engine of agroforestry is the subterranean mycorrhizal fungal network. Fungal hyphae colonize plant root systems, extending the root surface area by hundreds of times. (21) [ _________ ]. In exchange for carbon and carbohydrates produced via photosynthesis, these subterranean fungal conduits deliver dissolved phosphorus and micronutrients locked deep within mineral subsoils.

Furthermore, research demonstrates that mature trees actively share resources with neighboring shallow-rooted annual crops during seasonal drought. Deep oak and walnut roots pull moisture from deep water tables and release excess moisture into upper soil horizons through hydraulic lift. (22) [ _________ ]. Consequently, companion crops such as wheat or legumes withstand prolonged dry spells with significantly lower mortality.

Biological pest control also benefits from the multi-tiered canopy structure of agroforestry systems. Intercropped tree rows provide permanent overwintering nesting sites for insectivorous songbirds, bats, and predatory beetles. (23) [ _________ ]. As natural predator populations stabilize, chemical pesticide applications can be reduced by more than seventy percent without sacrificing crop yield.

Transitioning from monoculture to agroforestry is undeniably an investment in generational patience. Nut and timber trees require five to ten years of vegetative growth before yielding significant harvest revenue. (24) [ _________ ]. For land stewards seeking long-term resilience against climatic volatility, agroforestry provides an ecologically sound blueprint.
task_7_gapped_sentences.optionsReference:

[B] Timber harvesting machinery has become considerably more expensive due to rising diesel fuel tariffs.
[C] This symbiotic trade provides vital nourishment that plants cannot access independently.
[D] In response, an expanding international movement is championing precision agroforestry.
[E] This nocturnal moisture redistribution hydrates the surrounding shallow root zones.
[F] Chemical fertilizer runoff frequently contaminates freshwater river systems.
[G] However, the compounding ecological and economic dividends easily surpass short-term commercial forestry returns.

task_7_gapped_sentences.title: Living Lanterns of the Deep [Variant 16]
task_7_gapped_sentences.instruction: Read the text about bioluminescence. Choose the correct sentence from A–H to fit each gap (20–24).
task_7_gapped_sentences.passage:
In the pitch-black waters of the deep ocean, sunlight disappears entirely beyond two hundred meters. Yet this abyssal zone is far from completely dark; it sparkles with an astonishing array of living light. Bioluminescence—the biochemical production of light by living organisms—is not a rare curiosity, but the dominant mode of communication in the pelagic realm. (20) [ _________ ].

The chemical reaction powering this illumination typically involves two components: a light-emitting pigment called luciferin and an enzyme known as luciferase. When catalyzed in the presence of oxygen, this reaction releases almost ninety-eight percent of its energy as visible cold light, generating virtually no wasted heat. (21) [ _________ ]. In the open ocean, blue-green wavelengths travel farthest through seawater, which explains why the overwhelming majority of marine light displays conform to this color spectrum.

Marine creatures deploy bioluminescence for a wide spectrum of survival strategies. Many predatory anglerfish dangle glowing fleshy lures directly above their needle-sharp jaws to entice unsuspecting prey. (22) [ _________ ]. By emitting faint light from their bellies that precisely matches the intensity and wavelength of downwelling sunlight, midwater squid render their silhouettes invisible to predators lurking beneath them.

Other species utilize sudden, blinding flashes as an emergency defensive smokescreen. Deep-sea comb jellies and brittle stars discharge clouds of glowing mucus to disorient attackers while they make their escape. (23) [ _________ ]. This alarm summons even larger apex predators to attack the initial assailant, effectively saving the glowing prey in the chaos.

Today, biomedical researchers are adapting these natural light-generating systems for human healthcare. By inserting jellyfish bioluminescent genes into human cancer cells, oncologists can track tumor growth and evaluate drug effectiveness in real time under specialized microscopes. (24) [ _________ ]. What began as an evolutionary adaptation in deep-sea obscurity has transformed into an indispensable beacon illuminating modern medicine.
task_7_gapped_sentences.optionsReference:
[A] In some cases, this luminous display functions as a "burglar alarm" that attracts secondary predators.
[B] This thermal efficiency outstrips even the most advanced human-engineered LED technologies.
[C] In contrast, terrestrial fireflies utilize green-yellow flashes primarily for nocturnal courtship displays.
[D] Marine mammals, such as sperm whales, have never been observed producing bioluminescent chemicals.
[E] Marine scientists estimate that more than three-quarters of all midwater animals possess light-generating organs.
[F] Commercial fisheries frequently deploy synthetic chemical glow-sticks to attract schooling tuna.
[G] Similar genetic techniques are now being piloted to monitor wastewater contamination and bacterial pathogens.
[H] Equally widespread is the defensive tactic of counter-illumination camouflage.

task_7_gapped_sentences.title: The Phantom Islands of Early Sea Charts [Variant 22]
task_7_gapped_sentences.instruction: Choose the correct sentence (A–H) for each gap (20–24).
task_7_gapped_sentences.passage:
For hundreds of years, maritime navigators set sail across open oceans guided by maps depicting islands that did not exist. These elusive geographic ghosts occupied prominent positions on European charts from the fourteenth through the nineteenth centuries. (20) [ _________ ].

One famous example was Hy-Brasil, an enigmatic island said to lie west of Ireland. Celtic folklore held that it was perpetually cloaked in dense mists, revealing its shores once every seven years. (21) [ _________ ]. Admiralty charts marked its coordinates well into the Victorian era, as captains mistook low-hanging cloud banks for land.

Another enduring phantom was the island of Saint Brendan, named after a sixth-century Irish monk who sailed into the western ocean. Medieval cartographers placed Brendan's paradise across various Atlantic locations. (22) [ _________ ]. When Columbus set sail in 1492, his crew kept a vigilant watch for Brendan’s island as a provisioning post.

The persistence of these landmasses was not purely imagination; navigation was plagued by dead reckoning errors. (23) [ _________ ]. Furthermore, mapmakers faced intense commercial pressure to produce comprehensive charts; omitting an island claimed by a celebrated captain could ruin an atlas maker's reputation.

The ultimate demise of phantom islands arrived with the marine chronometer and systematic hydrographic surveying. (24) [ _________ ]. Yet, even today, these vanished archipelagos retain an enduring allure, reminding us of an era when the edges of maps were still inscribed with mystery.

task_7_gapped_sentences.title: The Chemistry of Illuminated Manuscript Preservation [Variant 24]
task_7_gapped_sentences.instruction: Read the text about historical manuscript conservation. Choose the correct sentence from A–G to fit each gap (20–24). There are two extra sentences.
task_7_gapped_sentences.passage:
Medieval illuminated manuscripts represent some of humanity's most visually stunning and fragile cultural artifacts. Crafted from animal vellum and decorated with ground mineral pigments and gold leaf, these books have survived for centuries in monastic vaults. (20) [ _________ ]. As conservation science matures, specialists are turning to non-destructive chemical analysis to decelerate this deterioration.

One of the primary agents of destruction is iron gall ink, which served as the standard writing medium across Europe from the Middle Ages through the nineteenth century. Created by combining iron sulfate with oak gall extracts, the ink produces a rich, durable dark line. (21) [ _________ ]. Over centuries, excess sulfuric acid eats entirely through the vellum substrate, causing text lines to crumble into brittle lacework.

To combat this corrosive pathway, conservators previously bathed entire folios in chemical neutralizing washes. (22) [ _________ ]. Early aqueous immersions frequently caused organic binder adhesives to dissolve, leading to catastrophic flaking of delicate illuminated gilding.

Modern preservation protocols therefore avoid invasive chemical baths whenever possible. Instead, technicians deploy non-invasive portable X-ray fluorescence (XRF) spectroscopy to map elemental distributions across the ink without physical contact. (23) [ _________ ]. Armed with this quantitative diagnostic map, conservators can pinpoint precisely which areas require micro-targeted antioxidant consolidation.

Environmental climate control remains the final, and most critical, line of defense. By maintaining storage vaults at a strict forty-five percent relative humidity and fifteen degrees Celsius, institutions prevent both vellum cockling and fungal germination. (24) [ _________ ]. Through this convergence of chemistry and microclimate management, these ancient voices will endure for future generations.

task_7_gapped_sentences.title: Precision Agroforestry and Soil Mycorrhizal Networks [Variant 25]

For decades, conventional industrial agriculture has relied on intensive monoculture cropping sustained by artificial nitrogen fertilizers and chemical fungicides. While this model initially delivered high crop yields, it has severely depleted topsoil biodiversity worldwide. (20) [ _________ ]. By integrating deep-rooted perennial trees directly into arable crop fields, farmers are restoring subterranean ecological synergy.

The foundational engine of agroforestry is the subterranean mycorrhizal fungal network. Fungal hyphae colonize plant root systems, extending the root surface area by hundreds of times. (21) [ _________ ]. In exchange for carbon and carbohydrates produced via photosynthesis, these subterranean fungal conduits deliver dissolved phosphorus and micronutrients locked deep within mineral subsoils.

Furthermore, research demonstrates that mature trees actively share resources with neighboring shallow-rooted annual crops during seasonal drought. Deep oak and walnut roots pull moisture from deep water tables and release excess moisture into upper soil horizons through hydraulic lift. (22) [ _________ ]. Consequently, companion crops such as wheat or legumes withstand prolonged dry spells with significantly lower mortality.

Biological pest control also benefits from the multi-tiered canopy structure of agroforestry systems. Intercropped tree rows provide permanent overwintering nesting sites for insectivorous songbirds, bats, and predatory beetles. (23) [ _________ ]. As natural predator populations stabilize, chemical pesticide applications can be reduced by more than seventy percent without sacrificing crop yield.

Transitioning from monoculture to agroforestry is undeniably an investment in generational patience. Nut and timber trees require five to ten years of vegetative growth before yielding significant harvest revenue. (24) [ _________ ]. For land stewards seeking long-term resilience against climatic volatility, agroforestry provides an ecologically sound blueprint.

task_8_gapped_paragraphs.title: The Architecture of Silence
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.instruction: Read the text about acoustic ecology. Choose the correct paragraph from A–F for each gap (25–29).
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.passage:
We inhabit an increasingly deafening civilization. From the perpetual hum of highway traffic to the relentless background churn of ventilation units, anthropogenic noise has permeated virtually every terrestrial ecosystem. While industrial noise was historically treated as an inevitable byproduct of economic progress, acoustic ecologists now recognize chronic sonic saturation as an insidious pollutant that fragments natural habitats and compromises human health.

(25) [ _________ ]

Field studies in national parks have documented this acoustic displacement in striking detail. In coniferous forests bordered by highways, songbirds are forced to alter their singing frequencies or elevate their vocal volume—a phenomenon known as the Lombard effect—merely to communicate territorial boundaries and attract mates. For species unable to shift their acoustic pitch, the consequences are dire: breeding success plummets, and entire populations abandon otherwise pristine nesting grounds.

(26) [ _________ ]

In urban centers, the human consequences of this acoustic assault are equally profound. Epidemiological research links long-term exposure to urban noise with sleep disturbance, impaired cognitive development in children, and heightened risks of cardiovascular disease. The human auditory system never sleeps; even during unconsciousness, the brain processes ambient decibels, interpreting sudden spikes as evolutionary alarm signals that trigger elevated heart rates and stress hormone release.

(27) [ _________ ]

Rather than viewing soundproofing solely as an engineering chore of building thicker walls, visionary planners are embracing "positive soundscape design." This methodology involves strategically integrating natural acoustic elements into civic architecture. Flowing water in civic plazas, gravel walkways, and rustling native foliage do not eliminate decibels, but mask harsh mechanical frequencies with restorative auditory cues.

(28) [ _________ ]

Furthermore, international legal frameworks are beginning to reflect this acoustic consciousness. Several European municipalities have established designated "Quiet Areas" where motor vehicle access is curtailed, and commercial developments must undergo rigorous acoustic impact audits before receiving construction permits.

(29) [ _________ ]

Preserving the integrity of natural soundscapes is not a sentimental indulgence; it is a fundamental pillar of ecological stewardship and human dignity in an overstimulated century.

task_8_gapped_paragraphs.title: Unchaining the Rivers: European Re-Wilding
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.instruction: Choose the correct paragraph (A–F) for each gap (25–29).
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.passage:
For over two centuries, European engineers treated natural rivers as hydrological threats. Meandering waterways were straightened into concrete channels, floodplains diked off, and thousands of weirs erected. While this spurred industrial growth, the ecological toll was catastrophic: riverine biodiversity collapsed by over eighty percent.

(25) [ _________ ]

This movement, broadly termed "river re-wilding," is founded upon a radical philosophical pivot: recognizing that a healthy river is a dynamic, self-healing entity. By dismantling derelict dams and allowing rivers to reclaim their historic paths, ecologists restore natural hydraulic dynamism.

(26) [ _________ ]

The speed of ecological recovery following barrier removal has astonished biologists. Within months of demolishing obsolete weirs, long-absent migratory species like Atlantic salmon and sea trout return to spawn in freshly exposed gravel beds.

(27) [ _________ ]

A quintessential catalyst in this restoration process is the reintroduction of Eurasian beavers. As natural ecological engineers, beavers construct permeable wood dams that create intricate wetland mosaics. Far from causing disastrous floods, these beaver ponds act as giant landscape sponges, capturing sediment and buffering surrounding farmland against severe droughts and flash flooding.

(28) [ _________ ]

Crucially, river re-wilding offers immense benefits for human settlements downstream. Traditional concrete flood channels actually exacerbate urban disaster by shooting storm surges downriver at unnatural velocities. Re-connected floodplains absorb massive flood peaks harmlessly upstream.

(29) [ _________ ]

In letting our rivers run wild once more, we are discovering that nature's ancient hydrological architecture remains infinitely wiser than our most sophisticated concrete fortifications.

task_8_gapped_paragraphs.title: The Philosophical Evolution of Cartography
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.instruction: Read the essay on cartography and epistemology. Choose the correct paragraph from A–F to fit each gap (25–29). There is one extra paragraph.
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.passage:
Maps are commonly regarded as objective, scientific mirrors of physical geography. When modern travellers glance at smartphone navigation screens, they operate under the intuitive assumption that satellite coordinates and digital cartography present an unmediated depiction of terrain. Yet historians of science have long demonstrated that cartography is never a purely passive reflection of reality; it is an active act of visual rhetoric and political assertion.

[ Paragraph Gap 25 ]

During the European Renaissance, maritime expansion demanded a transition from theological symbolism to functional navigational geometry. Navigators setting sail into open ocean could no longer rely on aesthetic coastline sketches. This operational necessity culminated in the landmark 1569 world map by Gerardus Mercator, which resolved a vexing mathematical challenge: how to project the surface of a spherical planet onto a flat sheet of parchment while preserving constant compass bearings as straight lines.

[ Paragraph Gap 26 ]

However, this mathematical convenience came with an enormous optical distortion that profoundly shaped geopolitics for centuries. Because the Mercator projection inflates landmasses progressively as they approach the poles, equatorial continents appear drastically diminished. Greenland appears equivalent in size to Africa, despite the African continent being fourteen times larger. For generations of schoolchildren and colonial administrators, this visual distortion reinforced Eurocentric imperial ideologies by exaggerating the territorial prominence of northern imperial powers.

[ Paragraph Gap 27 ]

This critique gained significant traction in the 1970s with the publication of the Peters projection, which prioritized proportional land area over navigational angles. While cartographers debated its aesthetic inelegance, the controversy successfully exposed mapmaking as an epistemological battleground. Maps were finally recognized by the general public not as immutable facts, but as selective arguments designed to serve specific societal priorities.

[ Paragraph Gap 28 ]

Digital geospatial algorithms now curate what information is rendered visible or omitted based on corporate profitability. A search query for an urban district highlights sponsored retail establishments and highway arteries, while obscuring historical landmarks, informal settlements, and low-income residential tracts. The digital map presents a seamless, authoritative veneer, yet it subtly conditions users to perceive urban space through a commercial lens.

[ Paragraph Gap 29 ]

Ultimately, cartography must be understood as an exercise in ethical discernment. To read a map critically is to interrogate what has been centered, what has been pushed to the periphery, and whose interests are legitimized by its boundaries.
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.optionsReference:
[A] In medieval Europe, for instance, the dominant map format was the 'T-O map', which organized the known world not around geographic scale, but around biblical dogma. Jerusalem occupied the exact geometrical center, East was situated at the summit, and vast uncharted continents were populated with mythological monsters, reflecting religious cosmology rather than empirical measurement.
[B] The solution lay in cylindrical projection geometry, where lines of latitude were spaced progressively wider toward the poles. While this mathematical innovation allowed sailors to draw simple straight lines for navigation routes without recalculating curvature, it introduced profound area distortions.
[C] Today, in the era of algorithmic digital mapping, this ideological mediation has not vanished; it has merely migrated into software code.
[D] Several polar expeditions suffered catastrophic failures after attempting to navigate uncharted arctic ice shelves with outdated magnetic compasses.
[E] Post-colonial geographers seized upon these distortions to demonstrate that maps had served as instruments of territorial domination, naturalizing political inequality through deceptive spatial scaling.
[F] By shedding the illusion of mathematical neutrality, modern mapmakers began acknowledging the socio-political responsibilities inherent in visualizing territorial boundaries.

task_8_gapped_paragraphs.title: Deep-Time Stratigraphy and the Anthropocene
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.instruction: Read the geological critique on deep time and Earth history. Choose the correct paragraph from A–F to fit each gap (25–29). There is one extra paragraph.
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.passage:
Geological time scales operate on an unimaginably vast horizon compared to human historical chronicles. The rock strata beneath our feet record four and a half billion years of volcanic cataclysms, continental collisions, and evolutionary transformations. Stratigraphers divide this unfathomable expanse into standardized units—eons, eras, periods, and epochs—demarcated by physical shifts in rock composition and fossilized bio-markers.

[ Paragraph Gap 25 ]

Traditionally, establishing a new geological epoch requires locating a Global Boundary Stratotype Section and Point (GSSP), informally known as a 'golden spike'. This physical rock outcrop must exhibit an unambiguous, globally synchronous geochemical or paleontological signal that can be recognized in sediment cores across continents for millions of years into deep time.

[ Paragraph Gap 26 ]

Yet in 2000, Nobel laureate Paul Crutzen proposed an unprecedented departure from standard stratigraphic conventions. He argued that human industrial activity has permanently altered the Earth's biogeochemical cycles to such an extent that the current Holocene epoch has come to an end, succeeded by a new epoch: the Anthropocene.

[ Paragraph Gap 27 ]

Advocates of formalizing the Anthropocene pointed to distinct mid-twentieth-century geochemical markers associated with the 'Great Acceleration'. Chief among these was radioactive fallout from atmospheric thermonuclear detonations in the early 1950s, which deposited synthetic plutonium isotopes globally in ocean sediments, glacial ice, and lakebeds.

[ Paragraph Gap 28 ]

However, the International Commission on Stratigraphy recently voted against officially adding the Anthropocene to the standard geological time scale. Stratigraphic traditionalists argued that human impact is an ongoing, non-synchronous diachronic process spanning millennia of deforestation and agriculture, rather than a single neat boundary stratum.

[ Paragraph Gap 29 ]

Whether classified as a formal geological epoch or an ongoing environmental crisis, the concept of the Anthropocene has fundamentally reshaped human self-understanding. It reminds civilization that human actions are no longer merely cultural, but are now operating as a planetary geologic force.

[B] To establish such markers, geologists conduct deep core drilling in secluded meromictic lakes where undisturbed varved sediments accumulate without biological disruption.
[C] This proposal sparked fierce contention within the scientific community, pitting conservative field stratigraphers against Earth systems scientists seeking to sound the alarm on global climatic disruption.
[D] Commercial mining conglomerates have heavily lobbied environmental ministries to halt the designated protection of pristine mineral reserves.
[E] Alongside these isotopic markers, synthetic plastics, fly ash particulates from coal combustion, and accelerated mass extinction rates created an unmistakable synthetic signature.
[F] They maintained that categorizing human transformation as an informal 'geological event'—akin to the Great Oxygenation Event—better captures its sprawling, uneven ecological reality.

task_8_gapped_paragraphs.title: The Philosophical Evolution of Cartography [Variant 9]
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.instruction: Read the essay on cartography and epistemology. Choose the correct paragraph from A–F to fit each gap (25–29). There is one extra paragraph.
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.passage:
Maps are commonly regarded as objective, scientific mirrors of physical geography. When modern travellers glance at smartphone navigation screens, they operate under the intuitive assumption that satellite coordinates and digital cartography present an unmediated depiction of terrain. Yet historians of science have long demonstrated that cartography is never a purely passive reflection of reality; it is an active act of visual rhetoric and political assertion.

[ Paragraph Gap 25 ]

During the European Renaissance, maritime expansion demanded a transition from theological symbolism to functional navigational geometry. Navigators setting sail into open ocean could no longer rely on aesthetic coastline sketches. This operational necessity culminated in the landmark 1569 world map by Gerardus Mercator, which resolved a vexing mathematical challenge: how to project the surface of a spherical planet onto a flat sheet of parchment while preserving constant compass bearings as straight lines.

[ Paragraph Gap 26 ]

However, this mathematical convenience came with an enormous optical distortion that profoundly shaped geopolitics for centuries. Because the Mercator projection inflates landmasses progressively as they approach the poles, equatorial continents appear drastically diminished. Greenland appears equivalent in size to Africa, despite the African continent being fourteen times larger. For generations of schoolchildren and colonial administrators, this visual distortion reinforced Eurocentric imperial ideologies by exaggerating the territorial prominence of northern imperial powers.

[ Paragraph Gap 27 ]

This critique gained significant traction in the 1970s with the publication of the Peters projection, which prioritized proportional land area over navigational angles. While cartographers debated its aesthetic inelegance, the controversy successfully exposed mapmaking as an epistemological battleground. Maps were finally recognized by the general public not as immutable facts, but as selective arguments designed to serve specific societal priorities.

[ Paragraph Gap 28 ]

Digital geospatial algorithms now curate what information is rendered visible or omitted based on corporate profitability. A search query for an urban district highlights sponsored retail establishments and highway arteries, while obscuring historical landmarks, informal settlements, and low-income residential tracts. The digital map presents a seamless, authoritative veneer, yet it subtly conditions users to perceive urban space through a commercial lens.

[ Paragraph Gap 29 ]

Ultimately, cartography must be understood as an exercise in ethical discernment. To read a map critically is to interrogate what has been centered, what has been pushed to the periphery, and whose interests are legitimized by its boundaries.
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.optionsReference:
[A] In medieval Europe, for instance, the dominant map format was the 'T-O map', which organized the known world not around geographic scale, but around biblical dogma. Jerusalem occupied the exact geometrical center, East was situated at the summit, and vast uncharted continents were populated with mythological monsters, reflecting religious cosmology rather than empirical measurement.
[B] The solution lay in cylindrical projection geometry, where lines of latitude were spaced progressively wider toward the poles. While this mathematical innovation allowed sailors to draw simple straight lines for navigation routes without recalculating curvature, it introduced profound area distortions.
[C] Today, in the era of algorithmic digital mapping, this ideological mediation has not vanished; it has merely migrated into software code.
[D] Several polar expeditions suffered catastrophic failures after attempting to navigate uncharted arctic ice shelves with outdated magnetic compasses.
[E] Post-colonial geographers seized upon these distortions to demonstrate that maps had served as instruments of territorial domination, naturalizing political inequality through deceptive spatial scaling.
[F] By shedding the illusion of mathematical neutrality, modern mapmakers began acknowledging the socio-political responsibilities inherent in visualizing territorial boundaries.

task_8_gapped_paragraphs.title: Deep-Time Stratigraphy and the Anthropocene [Variant 10]
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.instruction: Read the geological critique on deep time and Earth history. Choose the correct paragraph from A–F to fit each gap (25–29). There is one extra paragraph.
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.passage:
Geological time scales operate on an unimaginably vast horizon compared to human historical chronicles. The rock strata beneath our feet record four and a half billion years of volcanic cataclysms, continental collisions, and evolutionary transformations. Stratigraphers divide this unfathomable expanse into standardized units—eons, eras, periods, and epochs—demarcated by physical shifts in rock composition and fossilized bio-markers.

[ Paragraph Gap 25 ]

Traditionally, establishing a new geological epoch requires locating a Global Boundary Stratotype Section and Point (GSSP), informally known as a 'golden spike'. This physical rock outcrop must exhibit an unambiguous, globally synchronous geochemical or paleontological signal that can be recognized in sediment cores across continents for millions of years into deep time.

[ Paragraph Gap 26 ]

Yet in 2000, Nobel laureate Paul Crutzen proposed an unprecedented departure from standard stratigraphic conventions. He argued that human industrial activity has permanently altered the Earth's biogeochemical cycles to such an extent that the current Holocene epoch has come to an end, succeeded by a new epoch: the Anthropocene.

[ Paragraph Gap 27 ]

Advocates of formalizing the Anthropocene pointed to distinct mid-twentieth-century geochemical markers associated with the 'Great Acceleration'. Chief among these was radioactive fallout from atmospheric thermonuclear detonations in the early 1950s, which deposited synthetic plutonium isotopes globally in ocean sediments, glacial ice, and lakebeds.

[ Paragraph Gap 28 ]

However, the International Commission on Stratigraphy recently voted against officially adding the Anthropocene to the standard geological time scale. Stratigraphic traditionalists argued that human impact is an ongoing, non-synchronous diachronic process spanning millennia of deforestation and agriculture, rather than a single neat boundary stratum.

[ Paragraph Gap 29 ]

Whether classified as a formal geological epoch or an ongoing environmental crisis, the concept of the Anthropocene has fundamentally reshaped human self-understanding. It reminds civilization that human actions are no longer merely cultural, but are now operating as a planetary geologic force.

[B] To establish such markers, geologists conduct deep core drilling in secluded meromictic lakes where undisturbed varved sediments accumulate without biological disruption.
[C] This proposal sparked fierce contention within the scientific community, pitting conservative field stratigraphers against Earth systems scientists seeking to sound the alarm on global climatic disruption.
[D] Commercial mining conglomerates have heavily lobbied environmental ministries to halt the designated protection of pristine mineral reserves.
[E] Alongside these isotopic markers, synthetic plastics, fly ash particulates from coal combustion, and accelerated mass extinction rates created an unmistakable synthetic signature.
[F] They maintained that categorizing human transformation as an informal 'geological event'—akin to the Great Oxygenation Event—better captures its sprawling, uneven ecological reality.

task_8_gapped_paragraphs.title: The Architecture of Silence [Variant 16]
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.instruction: Read the text about acoustic ecology. Choose the correct paragraph from A–F for each gap (25–29).
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.passage:
We inhabit an increasingly deafening civilization. From the perpetual hum of highway traffic to the relentless background churn of ventilation units, anthropogenic noise has permeated virtually every terrestrial ecosystem. While industrial noise was historically treated as an inevitable byproduct of economic progress, acoustic ecologists now recognize chronic sonic saturation as an insidious pollutant that fragments natural habitats and compromises human health.

(25) [ _________ ]

Field studies in national parks have documented this acoustic displacement in striking detail. In coniferous forests bordered by highways, songbirds are forced to alter their singing frequencies or elevate their vocal volume—a phenomenon known as the Lombard effect—merely to communicate territorial boundaries and attract mates. (26) [ _________ ]

(27) [ _________ ]

Preserving the integrity of natural soundscapes is not a sentimental indulgence; it is a fundamental pillar of ecological stewardship and human dignity in an overstimulated century.

For over two centuries, European engineers treated natural rivers as hydrological threats. (29) [ _________ ]

task_8_gapped_paragraphs.title: The Philosophical Evolution of Cartography [Variant 19]
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.instruction: Read the essay on cartography and epistemology. Choose the correct paragraph from A–F to fit each gap (25–29). There is one extra paragraph.
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.passage:
Maps are commonly regarded as objective, scientific mirrors of physical geography. When modern travellers glance at smartphone navigation screens, they operate under the intuitive assumption that satellite coordinates and digital cartography present an unmediated depiction of terrain. Yet historians of science have long demonstrated that cartography is never a purely passive reflection of reality; it is an active act of visual rhetoric and political assertion.

[ Paragraph Gap 25 ]

During the European Renaissance, maritime expansion demanded a transition from theological symbolism to functional navigational geometry. Navigators setting sail into open ocean could no longer rely on aesthetic coastline sketches. This operational necessity culminated in the landmark 1569 world map by Gerardus Mercator, which resolved a vexing mathematical challenge: how to project the surface of a spherical planet onto a flat sheet of parchment while preserving constant compass bearings as straight lines.

[ Paragraph Gap 26 ]

However, this mathematical convenience came with an enormous optical distortion that profoundly shaped geopolitics for centuries. Because the Mercator projection inflates landmasses progressively as they approach the poles, equatorial continents appear drastically diminished. Greenland appears equivalent in size to Africa, despite the African continent being fourteen times larger. For generations of schoolchildren and colonial administrators, this visual distortion reinforced Eurocentric imperial ideologies by exaggerating the territorial prominence of northern imperial powers.

[ Paragraph Gap 27 ]

This critique gained significant traction in the 1970s with the publication of the Peters projection, which prioritized proportional land area over navigational angles. While cartographers debated its aesthetic inelegance, the controversy successfully exposed mapmaking as an epistemological battleground. Maps were finally recognized by the general public not as immutable facts, but as selective arguments designed to serve specific societal priorities.

[ Paragraph Gap 28 ]

Digital geospatial algorithms now curate what information is rendered visible or omitted based on corporate profitability. A search query for an urban district highlights sponsored retail establishments and highway arteries, while obscuring historical landmarks, informal settlements, and low-income residential tracts. The digital map presents a seamless, authoritative veneer, yet it subtly conditions users to perceive urban space through a commercial lens.

[ Paragraph Gap 29 ]

Ultimately, cartography must be understood as an exercise in ethical discernment. To read a map critically is to interrogate what has been centered, what has been pushed to the periphery, and whose interests are legitimized by its boundaries.

Jerusalem occupied the exact geometrical center, East was situated at the summit, and vast uncharted continents were populated with mythological monsters, reflecting religious cosmology rather than empirical measurement.
[B] The solution lay in cylindrical projection geometry, where lines of latitude were spaced progressively wider toward the poles. While this mathematical innovation allowed sailors to draw simple straight lines for navigation routes without recalculating curvature, it introduced profound area distortions.
[C] Today, in the era of algorithmic digital mapping, this ideological mediation has not vanished; it has merely migrated into software code.
[D] Several polar expeditions suffered catastrophic failures after attempting to navigate uncharted arctic ice shelves with outdated magnetic compasses.
[E] Post-colonial geographers seized upon these distortions to demonstrate that maps had served as instruments of territorial domination, naturalizing political inequality through deceptive spatial scaling.
[F] By shedding the illusion of mathematical neutrality, modern mapmakers began acknowledging the socio-political responsibilities inherent in visualizing territorial boundaries.

Digital geospatial algorithms now curate what information is rendered visible or omitted based on corporate profitability. A search query for an urban district highlights sponsored retail establishments and highway arteries, while obscuring historical landmarks, informal settlements, and low-income residential tracts. The digital map presents a seamless, authoritative veneer, yet it subtly conditions users to perceive urban space through a commercial lens.

[ Paragraph Gap 29 ]

Ultimately, cartography must be understood as an exercise in ethical discernment. To read a map critically is to interrogate what has been centered, what has been pushed to the periphery, and whose interests are legitimized by its boundaries.

[A] In medieval Europe, for instance, the dominant map format was the 'T-O map', which organized the known world not around geographic scale, but around biblical dogma. Jerusalem occupied the exact geometrical center, East was situated at the summit, and vast uncharted continents were populated with mythological monsters, reflecting religious cosmology rather than empirical measurement.
[B] The solution lay in cylindrical projection geometry, where lines of latitude were spaced progressively wider toward the poles. While this mathematical innovation allowed sailors to draw simple straight lines for navigation routes without recalculating curvature, it introduced profound area distortions.
[C] Today, in the era of algorithmic digital mapping, this ideological mediation has not vanished; it has merely migrated into software code.
[D] Several polar expeditions suffered catastrophic failures after attempting to navigate uncharted arctic ice shelves with outdated magnetic compasses.
[E] Post-colonial geographers seized upon these distortions to demonstrate that maps had served as instruments of territorial domination, naturalizing political inequality through deceptive spatial scaling.

task_8_gapped_paragraphs.title: Deep-Time Stratigraphy and the Anthropocene [Variant 25]
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.instruction: Read the geological critique on deep time and Earth history. Choose the correct paragraph from A–F to fit each gap (25–29). There is one extra paragraph.
task_8_gapped_paragraphs.passage:
Geological time scales operate on an unimaginably vast horizon compared to human historical chronicles. The rock strata beneath our feet record four and a half billion years of volcanic cataclysms, continental collisions, and evolutionary transformations. Stratigraphers divide this unfathomable expanse into standardized units—eons, eras, periods, and epochs—demarcated by physical shifts in rock composition and fossilized bio-markers.

[ Paragraph Gap 25 ]

Traditionally, establishing a new geological epoch requires locating a Global Boundary Stratotype Section and Point (GSSP), informally known as a 'golden spike'. This physical rock outcrop must exhibit an unambiguous, globally synchronous geochemical or paleontological signal that can be recognized in sediment cores across continents for millions of years into deep time.

[ Paragraph Gap 26 ]

Yet in 2000, Nobel laureate Paul Crutzen proposed an unprecedented departure from standard stratigraphic conventions. He argued that human industrial activity has permanently altered the Earth's biogeochemical cycles to such an extent that the current Holocene epoch has come to an end, succeeded by a new epoch: the Anthropocene.

[ Paragraph Gap 27 ]

Advocates of formalizing the Anthropocene pointed to distinct mid-twentieth-century geochemical markers associated with the 'Great Acceleration'. Chief among these was radioactive fallout from atmospheric thermonuclear detonations in the early 1950s, which deposited synthetic plutonium isotopes globally in ocean sediments, glacial ice, and lakebeds.

[ Paragraph Gap 28 ]

However, the International Commission on Stratigraphy recently voted against officially adding the Anthropocene to the standard geological time scale. Stratigraphic traditionalists argued that human impact is an ongoing, non-synchronous diachronic process spanning millennia of deforestation and agriculture, rather than a single neat boundary stratum.

[ Paragraph Gap 29 ]

Whether classified as a formal geological epoch or an ongoing environmental crisis, the concept of the Anthropocene has fundamentally reshaped human self-understanding. It reminds civilization that human actions are no longer merely cultural, but are now operating as a planetary geologic force.

[B] To establish such markers, geologists conduct deep core drilling in secluded meromictic lakes where undisturbed varved sediments accumulate without biological disruption.
[C] This proposal sparked fierce contention within the scientific community, pitting conservative field stratigraphers against Earth systems scientists seeking to sound the alarm on global climatic disruption.
[D] Commercial mining conglomerates have heavily lobbied environmental ministries to halt the designated protection of pristine mineral reserves.
[E] Alongside these isotopic markers, synthetic plastics, fly ash particulates from coal combustion, and accelerated mass extinction rates created an unmistakable synthetic signature.
[F] They maintained that categorizing human transformation as an informal 'geological event'—akin to the Great Oxygenation Event—better captures its sprawling, uneven ecological reality.

task_9_multiple_matching.title: The Blackwood Eco-Lodge: Four Guest Perspectives
task_9_multiple_matching.instruction: Read four reviews (A–D) of the Blackwood Eco-Lodge, and answer questions 30–33.
task_9_multiple_matching.passage:
Review A (Marcus): Having stayed at numerous wilderness retreats, I approached Blackwood with cautious optimism. What impressed me most was the transparency of their environmental commitments. Rather than indulging in superficial greenwashing, the management openly shares real-time solar generation metrics and gray-water recycling logs on monitors in the lobby. The guided dawn treks led by the resident botanist were a revelation, offering genuine insights into old-growth forest ecology. My sole reservation concerned the dining setup: the communal dinner tables, while evidently intended to cultivate social camaraderie, felt somewhat imposing after an exhausting day on the trails.

Review B (Claire): Blackwood offers an undeniably serene sanctuary from urban burnout, but prospective visitors must be prepared for true austerity. There are no charging outlets in the guest cabins, forcing a total digital detox that left several guests visibly agitated. While I personally appreciated the respite from screens, the evening lighting was so subdued that reading inside the cabin was practically impossible. That said, the kitchen staff deserves immense credit: every meal was prepared using seasonal produce harvested within ten miles of the property, showcasing culinary creativity that surpassed many Michelin-starred city bistros.

Review C (Julian): I booked Blackwood primarily for its remote location, hoping for complete solitude to finish writing a manuscript. In that respect, the lodge exceeded every expectation; the sound insulation between the timber cabins is remarkable, and waking up to panoramic mountain vistas without a combustion engine in earshot was revitalizing. However, I found the lodge’s pricing structure difficult to justify. While eco-conscious amenities certainly incur overheads, paying luxury hotel rates for off-grid shared shower blocks feels disproportionate, irrespective of how pristine the surrounding wilderness is.

Review D (Aisha): What sets Blackwood apart is its intimate relationship with the local village economy. Rather than operating as an isolated enclave for wealthy travelers, the lodge recruits exclusively from the surrounding rural community and purchases all timber furnishings from local craft cooperatives. You feel that your expenditure directly bolsters regional livelihoods. The activities program struck the perfect balance between strenuous adventure and mindful restorative downtime. I arrived thoroughly depleted and departed feeling physically invigorated and emotionally centered.

questions.trap: Marcus: 'the communal dinner tables... felt somewhat imposing after an exhausting day'.

questions.stem: 33. Which reviewer remarks on the exceptional standard of food despite strict sourcing limitations?
questions.trap: Claire: 'produce harvested within ten miles... culinary creativity that surpassed many Michelin-starred bistros'.

task_9_multiple_matching.title: The Custodians of Time: Four Restorers
task_9_multiple_matching.instruction: Match questions 30–33 with Restorers A–D.
task_9_multiple_matching.passage:
Restorer A (Horologist - Julian Vance): Restoring an 18th-century chiming pendulum clock is like unravelling a mechanical dialogue across centuries. If a brass tooth is worn down, I hand-file a replacement tooth from vintage brass alloy matching the era's metallurgy. The most humbling moment is hearing that steady heartbeat return after half a century of silence.

Restorer B (Bookbinder - Clara Thorne): People often imagine book restoration is about making a dilapidated volume look pristine. In reality, that scrubs away the history. When I mend torn rag-paper leaves, I use reversible wheat-starch paste. Every intervention must be completely reversible so future conservators can undo my work without harming the vellum.

Restorer C (Pipe Organ Voicer - Henrik Lindqvist): A pipe organ is an acoustic ecosystem breathing within an architectural cavern. You spend twelve hours a day perched atop wooden scaffolding inside a drafty cathedral shaving fractions of a millimeter from lead-tin lips. You aren't just tuning pitch; you are shaping timbre, breathiness, and attack.

Restorer D (Stained-Glass Glazier - Soraya Patel): Medieval stained glass is astonishingly fragile yet enduring. We clean panels with deionized water swabs and re-lead using historic alloy profiles. When afternoon sunlight streams through a conserved rose window, throwing sapphire refractions across stone floors, you understand why medieval worshippers believed light was divine.

questions.trap: Horologist Julian: 'replacement tooth from vintage brass alloy matching the era'.

questions.trap: Organ Voicer Henrik: 'perched atop wooden scaffolding in a drafty cathedral'.

questions.stem: 33. Which restorer reflects on how illumination creates an awe-inspiring visual experience?

task_9_multiple_matching.title: The Bridge Builders: Four Literary Translators
task_9_multiple_matching.instruction: Match questions 30–33 with Translators A–D.
task_9_multiple_matching.passage:
Translator A (Matteo - Italian Poetry): Translating verse is a daring act of poetic reincarnation. When tackling the hendecasyllables of Giacomo Leopardi, literal fidelity is the quickest route to aesthetic death. If you translate each word literally, you lose the rhythmic cadence, internal assonances, and musicality. My obligation is to re-create an equivalent aesthetic spell in English verse, even if that demands departing from surface syntax.

Translator B (Sunita - Postcolonial Fiction): My greatest ethical challenge is resisting the temptation to 'domesticate' foreign cultural idioms for Western readers. Replacing an indigenous culinary metaphor with a familiar British idiom sanitizes the text and imposes an imperial filter. Translation should intentionally leave subtle syntactic frictions intact; readers should be invited into a foreign rhythm of thought.

Translator C (Lukas - Historical Slavic Travelogues): Historical non-fiction requires an obsessive commitment to archival sleuthing. When translating an 18th-century explorer's diary across the Siberian taiga, you encounter obsolete navigational terms and fur trapper dialects. I spend weeks corresponding with forestry historians, maritime curators, and indigenous linguists just to identify a single referenced tree bark or knot.

Translator D (Elise - Avant-Garde Prose): Working with polyphonic, experimental novelists who deliberately fracture grammar is exhilarating. In an Argentine stream-of-consciousness novel, the author dispensed with punctuation. The challenge is capturing idiosyncratic cognitive momentum without smoothing out intentional roughness. A translated text should crackle with dangerous, rebellious energy.

questions.stem: 30. Which translator conducts extensive detective work with external academic specialists to verify historical terminology?
questions.trap: Translator C (Lukas): corresponds with forestry historians and museum curators.

questions.stem: 31. Which translator argues that capturing acoustic musicality takes precedence over literal word-for-word rendering?
questions.trap: Translator A (Matteo): literal fidelity loses rhythmic cadence and assonance.

questions.stem: 32. Which translator rejects the practice of sanitizing cultural idioms to make texts artificially familiar for Western readers?
questions.trap: Translator B (Sunita): refuses replacing indigenous metaphors with British idioms.

questions.stem: 33. Which translator relishes the challenge of preserving a writer's unconventional, grammatically fractured narrative voice?
questions.trap: Translator D (Elise): relishes capturing unconventional stream-of-consciousness momentum.

task_9_multiple_matching.title: Four Museum Curators on Digital Archiving & Repatriation
task_9_multiple_matching.instruction: Read the statements from four museum curators regarding cultural heritage preservation. For questions 30–33, choose from curators A–D.
task_9_multiple_matching.passage:
[A] Dr. Miriam Thorne — Digital Twin Specialist
"High-resolution 3D LiDAR scanning and photogrammetric micro-profiling allow us to construct hyper-accurate digital twins of vulnerable antiquities. While critics contend that digital files lack emotional aura, virtual replicas democratize scholarly access across global borders without exposing fragile originals to transport vibration or ambient moisture shock. Furthermore, if geopolitical conflict or seismic disasters threaten physical collections, digital archives preserve irreplaceable geometric and volumetric records for future conservationists."
[B] Julian Vance — Provenance Historian
"The true preservation crisis facing metropolitan museums is not physical decay, but moral and historical legitimacy. Decades of colonial acquisition records were intentionally obscured or sanitized in archival ledgers. Rigorous provenance research involves forensic archival tracking—uncovering purchase bills, expedition diaries, and military confiscation logs. Unless institutions confront the coercive circumstances of how objects were appropriated, technical conservation remains an evasion of ethical accountability."
[C] Dr. Kenji Sato — Community Custodianship Advocate
"Western museum models tend to treat sacred cultural artifacts as dead aesthetic specimens to be vacuum-sealed in climate-controlled glass vitrines. In many originating indigenous cultures, however, artifacts are living communal ancestors that require periodic ritual handling, natural weathering, and ceremonial activation. Repatriation cannot merely mean shipping boxes between government bureaucrats; it requires transitioning museum governance toward co-curation with originating descendant communities."
[D] Aris Thorne-Smith — Physical Materials Conservator
"Amid theoretical discourse on digital twins and political repatriation, we must not lose sight of fundamental material degradation. Ancient organic binders, polychrome pigments, and textile dyes undergo irreversible photolytic and chemical breakdown every hour they are exposed to gallery illumination. Without rigorous scientific stabilization, non-invasive consolidate coatings, and micro-climatic nitrogen enclosures, there will simply be nothing left of these physical artifacts for any community to claim or study."

questions.stem: 30. Which curator emphasizes that cultural artifacts should be engaged through living ritual practice rather than static display?
questions.trap: Dr. Sato: 'living communal ancestors that require periodic ritual handling'.

questions.stem: 31. Which curator highlights the protective value of 3D replication against unexpected catastrophic destruction?
questions.trap: Dr. Thorne: 'if geopolitical conflict or seismic disasters threaten physical collections'.

questions.stem: 32. Which curator insists that investigating historical acquisition methods is essential to institutional legitimacy?
questions.trap: Julian Vance: 'confront the coercive circumstances of how objects were appropriated'.

questions.stem: 33. Which curator warns that immediate physical decay threatens artifacts regardless of theoretical debates?
questions.trap: Aris Thorne-Smith: 'there will simply be nothing left of these physical artifacts for any community to claim'.

task_9_multiple_matching.title: Four Urban Planners on Next-Generation Commuter Infrastructure
task_9_multiple_matching.instruction: Read the viewpoints of four urban transportation planners regarding future metropolitan mobility. For questions 30–33, choose from planners A–D.
task_9_multiple_matching.passage:
[A] Nadia Rossi — Autonomous Light Rail Designer
"The future of mass transit lies in autonomous, on-demand light rail vehicles running on dedicated, grade-separated tracks. Unlike conventional subways that require billions in subterranean tunneling, modular elevated light rail can be rapidly erected over existing highway medians. By coordinating train frequency dynamically through predictive artificial intelligence, we eliminate timetable delays and slash energy waste during off-peak hours."
[B] Marcus Chen — Active Pedestrianization Strategist
"Technological fixes like autonomous cars or futuristic pods miss the core urban reality: geometry. Cities simply lack the physical ground space to accommodate personal vehicles, regardless of their propulsion source. The only scalable, health-affirming solution is aggressive street reallocation: stripping away multi-lane thoroughfares in favor of wide pedestrian promenades and physically protected cycle lanes. When walking and cycling become the safest, fastest travel modes, vehicular congestion vanishes naturally."
[C] Dr. Soren Lindqvist — Dynamic Congestion Pricing Econometrician
"Civic planners frequently ignore economic incentives. As long as urban road space is treated as a free public commons, motorists will inevitably overconsume it until gridlock ensues. Installing dynamic electronic toll gantries that adjust road usage charges in real time based on instantaneous traffic density immediately rationalizes demand. Revenues generated from peak congestion pricing can then be ring-fenced to subsidize regional bus transit for low-income commuters."
[D] Elena Rostova — Intermodal Suburban Hub Architect
"Metropolitan planners obsess over downtown city centers while ignoring suburban transit deserts where seventy percent of commuters actually reside. Our priority must be constructing intermodal park-and-ride interchanges at peripheral ring-road junctions. These hubs combine high-speed suburban express buses, electric vehicle charging depots, and micro-mobility rentals under one roof, providing a seamless bridge between sprawling residential neighborhoods and the urban core."

questions.stem: 30. Which planner argues that economic pricing mechanisms are needed to manage road usage efficiently?
questions.trap: Dr. Lindqvist: 'dynamic electronic toll gantries that adjust road usage charges in real time'.

questions.stem: 31. Which planner advocates for radical reallocation of street space to non-motorized transport?
questions.trap: Marcus Chen: 'stripping away multi-lane thoroughfares in favor of wide pedestrian promenades'.

questions.stem: 32. Which planner focuses on connecting suburban residential peripheries to central transit networks?
questions.trap: Elena Rostova: 'constructing intermodal park-and-ride interchanges at peripheral ring-road junctions'.

questions.stem: 33. Which planner highlights the construction and energy efficiency of AI-managed elevated rail?
questions.trap: Nadia Rossi: 'coordinating train frequency dynamically through predictive artificial intelligence'.

task_9_multiple_matching.title: The Bridge Builders: Four Literary Translators [Variant 13]
task_9_multiple_matching.instruction: Match questions 30–33 with Translators A–D.
task_9_multiple_matching.passage:
Translator A (Matteo - Italian Poetry): Translating verse is a daring act of poetic reincarnation. When tackling the hendecasyllables of Giacomo Leopardi, literal fidelity is the quickest route to aesthetic death. If you translate each word literally, you lose the rhythmic cadence, internal assonances, and musicality. My obligation is to re-create an equivalent aesthetic spell in English verse, even if that demands departing from surface syntax.

Replacing an indigenous culinary metaphor with a familiar British idiom sanitizes the text and imposes an imperial filter. Translation should intentionally leave subtle syntactic frictions intact; readers should be invited into a foreign rhythm of thought.

Translator C (Lukas - Historical Slavic Travelogues): Historical non-fiction requires an obsessive commitment to archival sleuthing. When translating an 18th-century explorer's diary across the Siberian taiga, you encounter obsolete navigational terms and fur trapper dialects. I spend weeks corresponding with forestry historians, maritime curators, and indigenous linguists just to identify a single referenced tree bark or knot.

Translator D (Elise - Avant-Garde Prose): Working with polyphonic, experimental novelists who deliberately fracture grammar is exhilarating. In an Argentine stream-of-consciousness novel, the author dispensed with punctuation. The challenge is capturing idiosyncratic cognitive momentum without smoothing out intentional roughness. A translated text should crackle with dangerous, rebellious energy.

questions.trap: Translator B (Sunita): refuses replacing indigenous metaphors with British idioms.

task_9_multiple_matching.title: Four Museum Curators on Digital Archiving & Repatriation [Variant 14]
task_9_multiple_matching.instruction: Read the statements from four museum curators regarding cultural heritage preservation. For questions 30–33, choose from curators A–D.
task_9_multiple_matching.passage:
[A] Dr. Miriam Thorne — Digital Twin Specialist
"High-resolution 3D LiDAR scanning and photogrammetric micro-profiling allow us to construct hyper-accurate digital twins of vulnerable antiquities. While critics contend that digital files lack emotional aura, virtual replicas democratize scholarly access across global borders without exposing fragile originals to transport vibration or ambient moisture shock. Furthermore, if geopolitical conflict or seismic disasters threaten physical collections, digital archives preserve irreplaceable geometric and volumetric records for future conservationists."
[B] Julian Vance — Provenance Historian
"The true preservation crisis facing metropolitan museums is not physical decay, but moral and historical legitimacy. Decades of colonial acquisition records were intentionally obscured or sanitized in archival ledgers. Rigorous provenance research involves forensic archival tracking—uncovering purchase bills, expedition diaries, and military confiscation logs. Unless institutions confront the coercive circumstances of how objects were appropriated, technical conservation remains an evasion of ethical accountability."
[C] Dr. Kenji Sato — Community Custodianship Advocate
"Western museum models tend to treat sacred cultural artifacts as dead aesthetic specimens to be vacuum-sealed in climate-controlled glass vitrines. In many originating indigenous cultures, however, artifacts are living communal ancestors that require periodic ritual handling, natural weathering, and ceremonial activation. Repatriation cannot merely mean shipping boxes between government bureaucrats; it requires transitioning museum governance toward co-curation with originating descendant communities."
[D] Aris Thorne-Smith — Physical Materials Conservator
"Amid theoretical discourse on digital twins and political repatriation, we must not lose sight of fundamental material degradation. Ancient organic binders, polychrome pigments, and textile dyes undergo irreversible photolytic and chemical breakdown every hour they are exposed to gallery illumination. Without rigorous scientific stabilization, non-invasive consolidate coatings, and micro-climatic nitrogen enclosures, there will simply be nothing left of these physical artifacts for any community to claim or study."

task_9_multiple_matching.title: The Custodians of Time: Four Restorers [Variant 22]
task_9_multiple_matching.instruction: Match questions 30–33 with Restorers A–D.
task_9_multiple_matching.passage:
Restorer A (Horologist - Julian Vance): Restoring an 18th-century chiming pendulum clock is like unravelling a mechanical dialogue across centuries. If a brass tooth is worn down, I hand-file a replacement tooth from vintage brass alloy matching the era's metallurgy. The most humbling moment is hearing that steady heartbeat return after half a century of silence.

Restorer B (Bookbinder - Clara Thorne): People often imagine book restoration is about making a dilapidated volume look pristine. In reality, that scrubs away the history. When I mend torn rag-paper leaves, I use reversible wheat-starch paste. Every intervention must be completely reversible so future conservators can undo my work without harming the vellum.

Restorer C (Pipe Organ Voicer - Henrik Lindqvist): A pipe organ is an acoustic ecosystem breathing within an architectural cavern. You spend twelve hours a day perched atop wooden scaffolding inside a drafty cathedral shaving fractions of a millimeter from lead-tin lips. You aren't just tuning pitch; you are shaping timbre, breathiness, and attack.

Restorer D (Stained-Glass Glazier - Soraya Patel): Medieval stained glass is astonishingly fragile yet enduring. We clean panels with deionized water swabs and re-lead using historic alloy profiles. When afternoon sunlight streams through a conserved rose window, throwing sapphire refractions across stone floors, you understand why medieval worshippers believed light was divine.

questions.trap: Bookbinder Clara: 'Every intervention must be completely reversible'.

questions.stem: 31. Which restorer sources period-accurate metals to ensure metallurgical authenticity?
questions.trap: Horologist Julian: 'replacement tooth from vintage brass alloy matching the era'.

questions.stem: 32. Which restorer describes the physical exertion of working in challenging architectural conditions?
questions.trap: Organ Voicer Henrik: 'perched atop wooden scaffolding in a drafty cathedral'.

questions.stem: 33. Which restorer reflects on how illumination creates an awe-inspiring visual experience?
questions.trap: Glazier Soraya: 'afternoon sunlight streams through freshly conserved rose window'.

task_9_multiple_matching.title: The Bridge Builders: Four Literary Translators [Variant 23]
task_9_multiple_matching.instruction: Match questions 30–33 with Translators A–D.
task_9_multiple_matching.passage:
Translator A (Matteo - Italian Poetry): Translating verse is a daring act of poetic reincarnation. When tackling the hendecasyllables of Giacomo Leopardi, literal fidelity is the quickest route to aesthetic death. If you translate each word literally, you lose the rhythmic cadence, internal assonances, and musicality. My obligation is to re-create an equivalent aesthetic spell in English verse, even if that demands departing from surface syntax.

Translator B (Sunita - Postcolonial Fiction): My greatest ethical challenge is resisting the temptation to 'domesticate' foreign cultural idioms for Western readers. Replacing an indigenous culinary metaphor with a familiar British idiom sanitizes the text and imposes an imperial filter. Translation should intentionally leave subtle syntactic frictions intact; readers should be invited into a foreign rhythm of thought.

Translator C (Lukas - Historical Slavic Travelogues): Historical non-fiction requires an obsessive commitment to archival sleuthing. When translating an 18th-century explorer's diary across the Siberian taiga, you encounter obsolete navigational terms and fur trapper dialects. I spend weeks corresponding with forestry historians, maritime curators, and indigenous linguists just to identify a single referenced tree bark or knot.

Translator D (Elise - Avant-Garde Prose): Working with polyphonic, experimental novelists who deliberately fracture grammar is exhilarating. In an Argentine stream-of-consciousness novel, the author dispensed with punctuation. The challenge is capturing idiosyncratic cognitive momentum without smoothing out intentional roughness. A translated text should crackle with dangerous, rebellious energy.

questions.stem: 30. Which translator conducts extensive detective work with external academic specialists to verify historical terminology?
questions.trap: Translator C (Lukas): corresponds with forestry historians and museum curators.

questions.stem: 31. Which translator argues that capturing acoustic musicality takes precedence over literal word-for-word rendering?
questions.trap: Translator A (Matteo): literal fidelity loses rhythmic cadence and assonance.

questions.stem: 32. Which translator rejects the practice of sanitizing cultural idioms to make texts artificially familiar for Western readers?
questions.trap: Translator B (Sunita): refuses replacing indigenous metaphors with British idioms.

questions.stem: 33. Which translator relishes the challenge of preserving a writer's unconventional, grammatically fractured narrative voice?
questions.trap: Translator D (Elise): relishes capturing unconventional stream-of-consciousness momentum.

task_9_multiple_matching.title: Four Museum Curators on Digital Archiving & Repatriation [Variant 24]
task_9_multiple_matching.instruction: Read the statements from four museum curators regarding cultural heritage preservation. For questions 30–33, choose from curators A–D.
task_9_multiple_matching.passage:
[A] Dr. Miriam Thorne — Digital Twin Specialist
"High-resolution 3D LiDAR scanning and photogrammetric micro-profiling allow us to construct hyper-accurate digital twins of vulnerable antiquities. While critics contend that digital files lack emotional aura, virtual replicas democratize scholarly access across global borders without exposing fragile originals to transport vibration or ambient moisture shock. Furthermore, if geopolitical conflict or seismic disasters threaten physical collections, digital archives preserve irreplaceable geometric and volumetric records for future conservationists."
[B] Julian Vance — Provenance Historian
"The true preservation crisis facing metropolitan museums is not physical decay, but moral and historical legitimacy. Decades of colonial acquisition records were intentionally obscured or sanitized in archival ledgers. Rigorous provenance research involves forensic archival tracking—uncovering purchase bills, expedition diaries, and military confiscation logs. Unless institutions confront the coercive circumstances of how objects were appropriated, technical conservation remains an evasion of ethical accountability."
[C] Dr. Kenji Sato — Community Custodianship Advocate
"Western museum models tend to treat sacred cultural artifacts as dead aesthetic specimens to be vacuum-sealed in climate-controlled glass vitrines. In many originating indigenous cultures, however, artifacts are living communal ancestors that require periodic ritual handling, natural weathering, and ceremonial activation. Repatriation cannot merely mean shipping boxes between government bureaucrats; it requires transitioning museum governance toward co-curation with originating descendant communities."
[D] Aris Thorne-Smith — Physical Materials Conservator
"Amid theoretical discourse on digital twins and political repatriation, we must not lose sight of fundamental material degradation. Ancient organic binders, polychrome pigments, and textile dyes undergo irreversible photolytic and chemical breakdown every hour they are exposed to gallery illumination. Without rigorous scientific stabilization, non-invasive consolidate coatings, and micro-climatic nitrogen enclosures, there will simply be nothing left of these physical artifacts for any community to claim or study."

questions.stem: 30. Which curator emphasizes that cultural artifacts should be engaged through living ritual practice rather than static display?
questions.trap: Dr. Sato: 'living communal ancestors that require periodic ritual handling'.

questions.stem: 31. Which curator highlights the protective value of 3D replication against unexpected catastrophic destruction?
questions.trap: Dr. Thorne: 'if geopolitical conflict or seismic disasters threaten physical collections'.

questions.stem: 32. Which curator insists that investigating historical acquisition methods is essential to institutional legitimacy?
questions.trap: Julian Vance: 'confront the coercive circumstances of how objects were appropriated'.

questions.stem: 33. Which curator warns that immediate physical decay threatens artifacts regardless of theoretical debates?
questions.trap: Aris Thorne-Smith: 'there will simply be nothing left of these physical artifacts for any community to claim'.

task_9_multiple_matching.title: Four Urban Planners on Next-Generation Commuter Infrastructure [Variant 25]
task_9_multiple_matching.instruction: Read the viewpoints of four urban transportation planners regarding future metropolitan mobility. For questions 30–33, choose from planners A–D.
task_9_multiple_matching.passage:
[A] Nadia Rossi — Autonomous Light Rail Designer
"The future of mass transit lies in autonomous, on-demand light rail vehicles running on dedicated, grade-separated tracks. Unlike conventional subways that require billions in subterranean tunneling, modular elevated light rail can be rapidly erected over existing highway medians. By coordinating train frequency dynamically through predictive artificial intelligence, we eliminate timetable delays and slash energy waste during off-peak hours."
[B] Marcus Chen — Active Pedestrianization Strategist
"Technological fixes like autonomous cars or futuristic pods miss the core urban reality: geometry. Cities simply lack the physical ground space to accommodate personal vehicles, regardless of their propulsion source. The only scalable, health-affirming solution is aggressive street reallocation: stripping away multi-lane thoroughfares in favor of wide pedestrian promenades and physically protected cycle lanes. When walking and cycling become the safest, fastest travel modes, vehicular congestion vanishes naturally."
[C] Dr. Soren Lindqvist — Dynamic Congestion Pricing Econometrician
"Civic planners frequently ignore economic incentives. As long as urban road space is treated as a free public commons, motorists will inevitably overconsume it until gridlock ensues. Installing dynamic electronic toll gantries that adjust road usage charges in real time based on instantaneous traffic density immediately rationalizes demand. Revenues generated from peak congestion pricing can then be ring-fenced to subsidize regional bus transit for low-income commuters."
[D] Elena Rostova — Intermodal Suburban Hub Architect
"Metropolitan planners obsess over downtown city centers while ignoring suburban transit deserts where seventy percent of commuters actually reside. Our priority must be constructing intermodal park-and-ride interchanges at peripheral ring-road junctions. These hubs combine high-speed suburban express buses, electric vehicle charging depots, and micro-mobility rentals under one roof, providing a seamless bridge between sprawling residential neighborhoods and the urban core."

questions.trap: Dr. Lindqvist: 'dynamic electronic toll gantries that adjust road usage charges in real time'.

questions.stem: 31. Which planner advocates for radical reallocation of street space to non-motorized transport?
questions.trap: Marcus Chen: 'stripping away multi-lane thoroughfares in favor of wide pedestrian promenades'.

questions.stem: 32. Which planner focuses on connecting suburban residential peripheries to central transit networks?
questions.trap: Elena Rostova: 'constructing intermodal park-and-ride interchanges at peripheral ring-road junctions'.

questions.stem: 33. Which planner highlights the construction and energy efficiency of AI-managed elevated rail?
questions.trap: Nadia Rossi: 'coordinating train frequency dynamically through predictive artificial intelligence'.
